0.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
0.overview:
First Thessalonians is probably the earliest of Paul’s letters preserved in the New Testament — penned from Corinth around AD 50–51, within just weeks or months of his departure from the Thessalonian church. It is a letter warm with affection, urgent with concern, and radiant with hope. More than almost any other letter in the Pauline corpus, it vibrates with the pulse of a young church under pressure and a pastor who loves them like a father, a mother, and a brother all at once.

The city of Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia — a major port, a commercial hub, a city full of every religion Rome and the East could offer. Paul had arrived there on his second missionary journey, preached for perhaps three weeks in the synagogue, and watched as a community of faith was born — Jewish converts, god-fearing Greeks, and not a few prominent women (Acts 17:1–9). Then a riot broke out, the city authorities were alarmed, and Paul was smuggled out by night. He never forgot those he had left behind.

The letter's great themes weave together like threads in a tapestry. There is the gospel — how it arrived in Thessalonica not merely as words but in power, in the Holy Spirit, in full conviction (1:5). There is the church as a community shaped by faith, hope, and love — Paul's great triad appears here earlier than in 1 Corinthians 13. There is holiness — the call to sanctification, especially in the realm of sexual purity, that flies directly in the face of Greco-Roman culture. And there is the return of Christ — the parousia — which dominates the last two chapters and gives the whole letter its eschatological urgency. The Thessalonians were grieving for those who had died before Jesus returned; Paul's answer is the most vivid description of the Second Coming in all of Scripture.

Above all, this is a letter about hope. Not the vague optimism the world calls hope, but the taut, muscular, resurrection-grounded hope that transforms how believers grieve, how they work, how they treat their bodies, and how they face the future. 'We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep,' Paul writes, 'so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope' (4:13). That contrast — hope versus hopelessness — is the heartbeat of 1 Thessalonians. The God who raised Jesus will raise them. The Lord who ascended will descend. The church that suffers now will be presented blameless before him at his coming.

1.title: The Gospel That Works
1.overview: This is probably the earliest letter in the New Testament, written around AD 50 from Corinth. Paul had preached in Thessalonica, capital of Macedonia, for only a few weeks before a riot forced him out by night (Acts 17:1–10). He had been frantic about the young church he left behind, and chapter 1 is his relief and thanksgiving at the news that they are standing. Its last line holds the whole Christian life: turned, serving, waiting.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter opens with the names of the three missionaries who founded the church, Paul, Silas and Timothy, and greets the believers as a congregation whose life is rooted in God the Father and the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Joining the Father and the Lord Jesus as a single source of grace and peace is a compressed confession of who Christ is, and its date makes it striking. Written around twenty years after the crucifixion, well before any Gospel, the letter already sets Jesus on God’s side of the line, stated as though it needed no defence.

A creature cannot be a co-source of divine blessing. If grace and peace come from Jesus in the same breath and under the same preposition as from the Father, then Jesus is not on the creature side of the line. The greeting is a doxology in miniature: two persons, one blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Thessalonica, kyrios (lord) was Caesar’s title, and the city was proud of its standing with Rome. The charge laid against these believers was that they said there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). A letter greeting them from the Lord Jesus reminded them whose throne their welfare actually came from.

Now: Where he was loved and trusted, Paul used no title, only his name. It is a fair question for anyone who holds office in a church: how much of your authority do you find you have to keep asserting, and why?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians is one of Paul’s earliest letters, written about AD 50–51 and, with James and Galatians, one of the usual candidates for the earliest book of the New Testament. It was sent to a church planted in a few weeks and then left suddenly under persecution. Paul writes to encourage them, answer slanders against him, teach them holiness, and comfort them about believers who had died before Christ’s return. Chapter 1 is a thanksgiving. Paul remembers their work of faith, labour of love and steadfastness of hope (vv. 1–3). He knows God chose them, because the gospel came with power, the Holy Spirit and deep conviction (vv. 4–5). They received the word with joy in suffering and became an example everywhere (vv. 6–8): they turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues from the coming wrath (vv. 9–10). It is a portrait of genuine conversion, and every line of it shows what God does.

The setting. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia, a busy port on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road from the Adriatic to Byzantium. Paul, Silas and Timothy came from Philippi, where Paul and Silas had been beaten with rods and jailed (Acts 16). They reasoned in the synagogue on three Sabbath days, and some Jews and a great many God-fearing Greeks believed. Then a jealous mob dragged Paul’s host Jason before the city authorities, and the believers sent Paul and Silas away by night (Acts 17:1–10). After perhaps a month the new church was on its own, with almost no teaching and no apostle. Paul sent Timothy back, and Timothy’s good report prompted this letter from Corinth (3:1–6; Acts 18:5): not a treatise but the relief of a man who had been sick with worry for a church he was forced to abandon.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. Paul does not call himself an apostle here. In Galatians and to the Corinthians the first line insists on it, because his authority was under attack; where he is loved and trusted he probably felt no need of the title. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts (Acts 15:40), whose feet were fastened in the stocks beside Paul’s in the Philippian jail and who sang hymns with him at midnight (Acts 16:24–25). Timothy is the young man from Lystra who will be sent back to Thessalonica alone, at some risk (3:2). All three had been in the city together, and Paul writes as one of a team.

In God the Father. The word church (ekklēsia) was the ordinary Greek word for an assembly, above all the gathering of a city’s citizens to do the town’s business. Paul gives it to a scattering of former idol-worshippers, weeks old, probably meeting in a house, in a town that had just run their teacher out, and then he tells them where they actually live: not the church at Thessalonica, but the church of the Thessalonians in God. Their address on earth was hostile; their address in heaven was the Father’s own life.

The Father and the Son under one preposition. The Father and the Lord Jesus Christ are joined as the single sphere in which the church lives, and Paul offers no explanation. No Jew raised on the Shema, the confession that the LORD our God is one, does that casually. In one of the earliest Christian sentences we possess, about twenty years after the cross, Jesus already stands on the divine side of the line. The church did not slowly promote a Galilean teacher to deity over centuries.

Grace to you and peace. This is the shortest of Paul’s greetings, and the order never varies, because it cannot. Grace is the unearned favour that comes down from God; peace is what it makes when it lands, peace with God and then the settled wholeness of a life put right. A church under pressure needs both, and in that order. Peace without grace is a truce that will not hold; grace always arrives carrying peace in its hands. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles have the shorter greeting.

What does it mean for a church to be in God? It means its existence and security rest in him, not in its numbers, building, reputation or leaders. A church in God is held by the Father’s care and joined to Christ as a body to its head, so its life comes from him and cannot be ended by the people who oppose it. Practically, it frees a small or struggling congregation from measuring itself by what the town thinks. The Thessalonian believers had no building, no history and no apostle, and Paul still addresses them as an assembly whose true location is the Father and the Son. Your church, however ordinary its Sunday looks, is that too.

Why does Paul leave out his apostleship here? Because nothing in Thessalonica required him to defend it. His authority was not in question, so he simply wrote as a friend alongside his fellow workers. It is a quiet lesson for anyone with a title: use it when the truth needs defending, and set it aside when love can do the work without it. Authority in the church is a trust for the good of others, not a badge to wear.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the Via Egnatia, Rome’s great east–west road. Paul founded the church on his second journey but was soon driven out. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul probably wrote from Corinth around AD 50, making this one of his earliest letters.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:2–10 – Faith, Love, Hope — and a Church Everyone Was Talking About
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for their faith, love and hope, and is sure God has chosen them, because the gospel reached them with the Spirit’s power. They welcomed it in persecution, with joy, and became a pattern for believers across Macedonia and Achaia, known everywhere for turning from idols to serve the true God and to wait for his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and how anyone could know

Paul claims no private glimpse of God’s decree. He reasons from effect to cause: the gospel arrived with power, the Spirit and settled conviction, and it produced work, labour and endurance; therefore God had chosen them. The hidden choice becomes visible in time through God’s effective call, which is why Peter can speak of making our calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:10).

Their faith and love are not the ground of their election, which lies wholly in God, but they are its evidence. And Paul uses the doctrine not to sort the congregation or to threaten, but to give persecuted people the one ground that cannot shift.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul had perhaps a month in the city (Acts 17:2) before a mob forced him out at night, yet within months this church was the pattern held up to older congregations across two provinces.

Now: The Thessalonians did not set out to be famous; what travelled was the report of changed, glad people. A church that wants to be heard of can learn from that: the reputation that carries the gospel is a by-product, not a campaign.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Always, all, constantly. Three words govern this verse. Paul had left this church in the worst possible circumstances and spent months, as chapter 3 tells, unable to bear the suspense. Thanksgiving was not his obvious response to Thessalonica; it was his settled one. And the thanks goes to God, not to the Thessalonians, because their faith is God’s work.

In the flow. Verses 2 to 5 are one long sentence in Greek. Paul gives thanks (v. 2), says what he remembers (v. 3), and says why he is sure these people belong to God (vv. 4–5). Most of Paul’s letters open with thanks, but here the thanks fills the whole chapter and breaks out again later (2:13; 3:9). Before he answers any slander or corrects anything, a relieved Paul tells a frightened church what God has already done in it.

For all of you. Not for the promising ones, or the ones who had held up best. Nobody is left out, because nobody in the church is there by his own achievement.

Constantly. The word means unceasingly, and Paul uses it three times in this short letter (1:2; 2:13; 5:17), more than anywhere else. It describes a habit, not a mood: this church came up every time he prayed, by name, because he could not stop thinking about them.

What Paul did with his worry. Paul is worried sick about these people and cannot reach them, and he turns the worry into thanksgiving and intercession. He does not brood, and he does not wait until the news is good. Anxiety about people you love is raw material: carry it to God, and begin with what God has already done in them.

A greater intercessor. Paul could do nothing for Thessalonica but pray from a distance, and his prayers mattered. Yet behind them stands an intercession that never breaks. Before he went to the cross, the Lord Jesus prayed not only for his apostles but for those who would believe in him through their word (John 17:20), and that included a company of former idol-worshippers in a Macedonian port. Now risen, he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). Paul mentions them constantly; Christ never stops. That is the deepest reason Paul can give thanks for a church he cannot reach: its life never hung on the apostle, but on the Son at the Father’s right hand.

How can I pray for people constantly when the list keeps growing? Pray regularly rather than exhaustively. Many Christians keep a short list for each day of the week, so that everyone comes round in turn, and then pray as people come to mind during the day, in a sentence, at the sink or on the bus. Begin, as Paul does, with thanks for what God has done in them, then ask for what they need. You will not pray for everyone every day, and you do not need to. What matters is that the people God has given you are not forgotten before him.

Why thank God, and not the person? Because faith, love and hope are gifts before they are achievements. It is right to encourage people, and Paul does so warmly in this very letter. But when you thank God for a brother’s faith, you are telling the truth about where it came from, and you keep both of you from pride.

verseByVerse.quote: remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remembering before our God and Father. In prayer Paul recalls what God has done in them, and here is the triad that will become famous, faith, love and hope, perhaps the earliest place it appears in writing. But look at what Paul attaches to each, because the nouns are doing the real work: the work of faith, the labour of love, the steadfastness of hope.

Your work of faith. Faith produces work. Not work that earns anything (Paul will spend Romans and Galatians demolishing that idea), but work that faith itself generates, as a live root pushes up a shoot (Galatians 5:6; James 2:18). A faith that has changed nothing about what you do is a faith Paul would not recognise.

And labour of love. Love produces labour. The word is kopos: toil to the point of weariness. Paul does not say love produces warm feeling; he says it produces the tiredness of doing something hard for somebody else. Most real love in a church looks like being worn out by people: the meals cooked, the hospital visits, the long conversation with someone who keeps returning to the same grief.

And steadfastness of hope. Hope produces steadfastness. The word is hypomonē, endurance: not passive resignation but the staying power of someone who keeps going under a weight without buckling. Hope is what makes endurance possible, not the other way round. You can bear almost anything if you know it ends, and how, and these persecuted believers were fed by what was coming: the return of Christ.

In our Lord Jesus Christ. The phrase governs the whole line. This is not a list of admirable human qualities; it is a description of what Christ produces in people joined to him. Joined means more than admiring him from a distance. By faith a believer is united to Christ as a branch is to a vine, so that his life flows into ours and bears fruit (John 15:5). Faith looks back to what Christ has done, love looks around to others for his sake, and hope looks forward to his coming. Paul returns to the three again and again (5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 1:4–5), and in every place they are held together by the one person they look to.

Is the work of faith the same as the works Paul rejects in Galatians? No. The works Paul rejects are works done to earn a right standing with God, as though our obedience could pay for acceptance. The work of faith is what faith does after God has freely accepted us in Christ: it trusts him, and so it obeys him, serves, forgives, and keeps going. The first is a wage; the second is a fruit. A Christian works hard, but from acceptance, not for it.

What if my love feels more like exhaustion than affection? Then you may be closer to this verse than you think. Paul chose the word for weary toil, not the word for warm feelings. Being tired from loving people is often a sign that love is real. But exhaustion also needs care: rest, prayer, and other believers sharing the load. Love that labours must also keep drawing from Christ, or it will curdle into resentment. Ask him for strength, and ask the church for help.

A test from the verse. Faith, love and hope are easy words and cost nothing to claim. Paul measures them by what they produce: work, weariness, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would be different if you did not. If that question troubles you, the trouble is itself a sign of life: dead faith does not worry about its fruit. None of us bears this fruit perfectly; Christ alone obeyed perfectly, in our place, and for his sake God accepts our flawed work. Bring the weak fruit to him, in whom all three grow; the Holy Spirit, now living in you, is the one who grows them.

For worship. Glory to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the root of all three. He is the one faith trusts, the one love serves, the one hope waits for. He makes weak people work, tired people love, and frightened people stand, and when the work is done, the labour spent and the waiting over, he himself will be the reward.
verseByVerse.note: Faith, love and hope — the triad Paul returns to again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers loved by God. Two enormous things are said here almost in passing, to a church perhaps six months old. The word (ēgapēmenoi) is a perfect passive participle: having been loved, and standing loved. It is a settled state, not a mood God is in on a good day, and it is the ground of their election, not anything in them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8; Ephesians 1:4–5). And brothers, used of the whole church, men and women together, tells people who had lost their families by turning from the gods that they have a new one.

That he has chosen you. The word is election (eklogē), the choosing out of some. To be elect is to have been chosen by God for salvation in Christ before the world began, for reasons that lay in his love and not in us. Paul states it flatly, as a comfort rather than a puzzle (2 Thessalonians 2:13). See where he puts this doctrine some find cold: in a letter to frightened people under persecution, as the first solid ground he can give them. If their standing rested on their own decision, a bad enough month could undo it. If it rests on his choice, it cannot.

How could Paul know? This is the question people ask in the car park afterwards. Election is a decree made in eternity, and no one has read the register. Paul is not claiming a private revelation. He tells us his evidence in the next word, because, and it runs straight into verse 5: he knows they were chosen because of how the gospel arrived among them and what it did when it arrived.

Where Christians differ: can we know who is elect? Some say election is unknowable and therefore irrelevant; others claim to know others’ eternal destiny. Some Christians (Arminians) hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe, out of sincere concern for God’s fairness; many are devoted servants of Christ. But Paul knows they were chosen because the gospel came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit (v. 5) and they received it: their faith is the evidence of God’s choice, not its cause. Verdict: Election is God’s free choice before the foundation of the world, not based on foreseen faith (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11). We cannot read God’s secret will directly, but election shows itself in its fruits: the gospel received with power and conviction, a turning from idols, faith, love and hope (vv. 3–10; 2 Peter 1:10). So believers may have assurance of their election, and the church may speak of believers as chosen, while leaving final judgement to God, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both teach (Westminster 3.8; 1689 3.7).

The pastoral shape of the doctrine. The root is hidden; the fruit is not (2 Peter 1:10). And Paul does not use election as a threat or to sort the congregation. He uses it the way you would hand a deed of title to a nervous tenant: this is yours, and here is why nobody can take it.

Chosen in the Beloved. Paul calls them loved by God, and the New Testament tells us where that love is found: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, and blessed us in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:4–6). The Father has one beloved Son (Matthew 3:17), and the election of the Thessalonians is their inclusion in his love for him. That is what makes it safe. They were not chosen as freestanding individuals whose record God keeps checking, but as people joined to the Son. What does that mean on a bad day? God’s love for you is as steady as his love for Jesus, because it is the same love (John 17:23).

I cannot see much fruit in my life. Does that mean I am not chosen? Look more carefully, and look at the right things. The fruit is not spiritual brilliance but the marks Paul lists: you have heard the gospel and believe it is true; you have turned, however falteringly, from what you once served; you love God’s people and want to be with them; you keep coming back to Christ when you fail. Weak faith in Christ is still faith in Christ. And remember that assurance is not first found by staring inward. Look to Christ, who invites everyone who comes to him and casts out none (John 6:37). Whoever comes is chosen; election is God’s explanation of why you came.

If God has chosen, why should I pray for unbelievers or share the gospel? Because God has chosen to save his people through prayer and preaching, and he gives us the privilege of being his means. Election is the reason evangelism is hopeful, not the reason it is pointless. In Corinth, when Paul was opposed, the Lord told him that he had many people in that city (Acts 18:10), and the promise kept him there preaching for eighteen months. We do not know who the elect are, so we tell everyone, and we pray expecting God to open hearts.

For worship. Before the world was made, God set his love on people who would one day bow to idols in a Greek port, and he did not change his mind when they did. He sent his Son to die for them, then a tired missionary to tell them, and the Spirit to open their ears. Not one link in that chain was forged by them, and not one can be broken by them. The love that began in eternity, passed through Golgotha and reached a Thessalonian workshop is the love that holds every believer still, and it will bring them all home.

verseByVerse.quote: because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not only in word. Here is Paul’s evidence, in two halves. The gospel came in word: it was preached, it had content, it was argued from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, and there is no gospel without words. But it did not come only in word.

In power and in the Holy Spirit. Words are the instrument, not the agent. Paul refuses to credit the result to his own delivery: the Spirit made the words effective and changed hearts (Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:4). Theologians call this effectual calling. The gospel’s outward call goes to everyone who hears it, but the Spirit’s inward call opens the heart, so that the hearer actually comes, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart in Philippi a few weeks earlier (Acts 16:14). The same sermon can leave one room unmoved and another in tears, and the difference is not the sermon.

And with full conviction. The word is plērophoria: settled, unhesitating certainty, carried all the way through. It probably covers both sides: the preachers spoke with full assurance, and the hearers received it so. The thing landed on them with the weight of fact.

What kind of men we proved to be. This half of the verse is often skipped. Paul points to the messengers themselves, and to what these people had watched: men who arrived with their backs still marked from a flogging in Philippi (2:2), who worked night and day at a trade so as not to burden anybody (2:9), and who were sent out of town when the mob came for them (Acts 17:10). The gospel came in the hands of men whose lives corroborated it, and even that was for your sake, aimed at them and not at Paul’s reputation. The Spirit gives the power; a life gives the credibility.

This Jesus is the Christ. What was the gospel that came with such power? Luke tells us what Paul argued in that synagogue: that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and that this Jesus, whom he proclaimed, is the Christ (Acts 17:3). The power came with a message about a crucified man, because the Spirit’s work is to glorify Christ, taking what is his and making it known (John 16:14). And the messengers fitted the message. Men with flogged backs, preaching a Messiah who suffered before he reigned, were living illustrations of what they said.

Does power mean miracles? Should we expect them when we preach? Paul may include the signs that accompanied the apostles’ ministry (Romans 15:19; 2 Corinthians 12:12), but his main point is the power that converts: the Spirit opening blind eyes to the truth of Christ. This commentary’s view is cessationist (the view that the miraculous sign-gifts ceased with the apostles), held charitably: the miraculous sign-gifts that authenticated the apostles and their message belonged to that founding period, while the Spirit’s converting power goes on in every age. The reason is that Scripture itself calls those signs the marks of an apostle and ties them to the first witnesses (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic, believe the gifts continue, and this commentary honours them as brothers and sisters. So yes, expect power when the gospel is preached, the greatest power there is: dead hearts made alive. That is a greater wonder than a healed body, and God still does it.

Was this full conviction just the excitement of a crowd? A sceptic will say so, and the question is fair, because crowds can be stirred to believe anything for an evening. But look at what this conviction did. It did not fade when the preachers left town by night; it held through months of hostility from neighbours and families (2:14), with no apostle to keep it warm. Crowd excitement needs the crowd. This needed nothing but the word and the Spirit, and it made people steady rather than giddy. That is why Paul treats it as the mark of God’s hand, not of a good meeting.

I have never preached a sermon. Does this verse apply to me? Yes. Every Christian who speaks of Christ to a friend, a child or a colleague does what Paul did on a smaller scale: speaks true words, depending on the Spirit to make them live, from a life that does not contradict them. You cannot supply the power, and you are not asked to. You are asked to say what is true, kindly and clearly, and to live so that your words are believable.

For worship. Praise to the Holy Spirit, who takes ordinary words from ordinary mouths and makes them the voice of God to a dead heart. He did it in a Thessalonian synagogue with an argument about a cross, and the people who heard it found themselves loving a man they had never seen (1 Peter 1:8). No preacher can make anyone love Christ. The Spirit has done it in multitudes, and every believer alive is his monument: a heart that first heard of the Son in plain words and then could not stop looking at him.

verseByVerse.quote: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imitators of us and of the Lord. They copied the missionaries, and through them the Lord himself, in one respect: not Paul’s gifts or his knowledge, but the way he took a beating and kept his joy. And behind Paul stands the Lord, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

They had seen him do it. These people had watched Paul preach with his back marked from Philippi, and some had watched him hustled out of town at night. When the same trouble came on them, they behaved the same way. Imitation in the New Testament is rarely copying a technique. It is having watched somebody under pressure and finding, when your turn comes, that you do what they did.

In much affliction. The word is thlipsis, pressure, the crushing weight. They believed in the middle of riots and opposition (Acts 17:5–9), and as chapter 2 will show, their own countrymen turned on them (2:14). This was real trouble, not inconvenience.

With the joy of the Holy Spirit. Not joy they worked up, and not the absence of pain, but something the Spirit produced while the pressure was still on (Acts 13:52). Affliction without joy is simply misfortune. Joy without affliction is cheap and proves nothing. Joy inside affliction is a fact that demands an explanation, and people go looking for one.

An example. The word is typos, first the impression a stamp leaves and then, in ordinary use, a pattern or model; our word type. The gospel had left its impression on them, and other churches could read it off them. Macedonia was the northern province, with Philippi and Beroea; Achaia was southern Greece, with Athens and Corinth.

Weigh how quickly this happened. Paul had been with them a matter of weeks. He is writing months later, and already this congregation of new converts is the pattern held up to the churches of two Roman provinces. Length of time in the faith and usefulness to God are not the same measurement.

Is it wrong to feel sad or afraid when I suffer? No. The Lord Jesus wept and was troubled in spirit, and Paul himself writes of grief and anxiety in this letter (2:17; 3:5). The joy of the Spirit is not a fixed smile or a denial of pain. It is a deeper gladness that Christ is yours and that nothing can take him from you, a joy that can sit beside sorrow and outlast it. If you cannot feel it today, ask for it; it is the Spirit’s gift, not your achievement.

Is it right to imitate human leaders? Yes, so far as they imitate Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Paul deliberately offered his life as a pattern, and God gives his church living examples because we learn best by watching. But the imitation always passes through the man to the Lord. Copy a Christian’s faith, patience and love; never make him your master, and never follow him where he departs from Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of one believer you have watched suffer well: what they said, what they refused to say, where they went for help. Someone may be watching you in your present difficulty in the same way, so ask the Holy Spirit for joy in the middle of it.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

verseByVerse.quote: For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sounded forth. The verb is exēcheō, from which we get echo, a word for a sound that rings out and carries, like a trumpet or rolling thunder. The gospel struck this church like a hammer on a bell, and the ringing went out across the province. The tense is perfect: it sounded and is still sounding.

Gone forth everywhere. Travellers, traders and sailors carried the story along the Via Egnatia. Everywhere is the natural exaggeration of delight: the report had gone far beyond where Paul could have taken it. The church did not organise this. What could be seen of them was simply worth repeating.

We need not say anything. Paul, whose vocation was saying things, arrives somewhere to talk about the gospel and finds people telling him about the Thessalonians first. He is delighted to be redundant.

What actually travelled. This is bracing for Christians who feel they have no gift for evangelism. What travelled was not a programme but a report: a group of people in Thessalonica had dropped their idols and would not stop being glad about it under pressure. Nobody set out to be famous across two provinces. They were simply visible. A reputation pursued for its own sake soon shapes the message to please the audience; one that comes as the by-product of changed lives points away from the church to the Lord who changed them.

The word of the Lord. The Lord here is most likely the Lord Jesus, as usually in Paul, and the word is his. Before he ascended he told his apostles they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8), and Paul reads the spread of the gospel in the words of Psalm 19: their voice has gone out to all the earth (Romans 10:18). What rang out from Thessalonica was the risen Christ keeping his promise. He had sent the gospel down the Via Egnatia with a hunted missionary; now he sent it back along the same road in the lives of the people it had reached.

Does every Christian have to evangelise? I am shy and not good with words. Every Christian is a witness, but not every Christian is a preacher. The Thessalonians spread the word first by being a visible, changed people, and then by speaking when people asked about it (1 Peter 3:15). You can do both. Live openly as a Christian, let people know you go to church and why, pray for the people around you, invite them to hear the gospel, and when someone asks why you have hope, tell them simply what Christ has done for you. The Lord uses quiet voices. Faithfulness, not eloquence, is what he asks.

Is the word of the Lord the Bible, or the spoken gospel? Here it is the gospel message about Christ, spoken and passed on. That message is the same word God has now given us, fixed and complete, in Scripture. What sounded out from Thessalonica was not new revelation from the church but the apostolic gospel the church had received, repeated faithfully.

verseByVerse.quote: For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What they report. This is one of the most compact summaries of conversion in the New Testament: a turning to, and a turning from.

Turned to God from idols. Toward God first, and from idols as the consequence. That is nearly always the real sequence: people rarely put down an idol because they have been persuaded it is worthless in the abstract, but because something better has taken hold of them. Reverse it and you get willpower, a short-lived fuel. And the phrase from idols tells us that most of this church were converted pagans, not Jews.

What it cost in that city. Thessalonica was thick with the worship of Dionysus, Serapis and the Cabiri and, most dangerously, of the emperor. Religion was civic membership: the trade guilds had patron gods and sacrificial meals, family life ran on household deities, and loyalty was measured by attendance. To turn from idols was to resign from the life of the town, which goes a long way to explain the affliction of verse 6.

To serve the living and true God. Both adjectives are aimed. An idol is not living: Isaiah mocked the man who burns half a tree to warm himself and worships the other half (Isaiah 44:14–17). And it is not true: it corresponds to nothing. Paul is using Jeremiah’s language for the LORD, the true God and the living God (Jeremiah 10:10), against exactly such rivals (Acts 14:15).

Serve. The verb is douleuō, to serve as a slave, and the blunt word is deliberate. They did not exchange servitude for independence; they changed owners. The question is never whether to serve something but which master is worth it, and only one of the available masters is alive. Only one of them died for his servants.

Him who is true. John closes his first letter with the same pair, the true God and idols, and shows where the true God is known: the Son of God has come and given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ (1 John 5:20–21). The Thessalonians did not turn from carved gods to a vaguer idea of the divine. They turned to the God who had shown his face in Jesus, which is why Paul’s next words are about his Son. People make idols in their own image. The living God made himself known by taking ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean modern people have no idols. Anything we trust, love or fear more than God is an idol (Colossians 3:5), whether or not it has a shrine.

How do I find my idols if I own no statues? Asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask instead what you serve: what you organise your week around, what you are afraid of losing, what you daydream about, what you would sacrifice sleep, money and integrity to keep, and what makes you angry or despairing when it is threatened. Good things become idols when we ask them to give us what only God can give: security, worth, comfort, control. That is the altar, whatever is or is not standing on it.

How do I actually turn from an idol? The same way the Thessalonians did: by turning to God first. Confess it to him by name. Then look hard at the living and true God, his goodness, his promises, his Son, until the idol looks small beside him. Cut off what feeds it where you can, and replace it with service: give away some of the money, use the time for others, bring the fear to God in prayer every time it rises. Expect to turn again and again. Old idols rarely leave in one day, but a heart that has seen the living God never fully goes back.

For worship. The idols of Thessalonica are dust, and the God the Thessalonians turned to is as alive as on the day they first heard of him. He is living, and he gives life; he is true, and he never deceives. The gods of the city had to be fed and gave nothing back. This God came looking for people who had bowed to wood and stone, opened his house to them, and set them at his table as sons. Glory to the living and true God, whose service is the only freedom there is.
verseByVerse.note: Turning “from idols” shows that most of the church were converted pagans, not Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To wait for his Son. Two verbs describe the Christian life here: to serve, and to wait. The waiting (anamenō) is not idleness but expectancy, like watching a road for someone you love. Within weeks of conversion these believers had been taught to live with their eyes on the horizon, and the second coming runs through every chapter of this letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:13–18; 5:1–11, 23).

Whom he raised from the dead. The return is not a hope hanging in mid-air. It rests on something that has already happened in public: the resurrection proves he is God’s Son and guarantees his return as Judge (Acts 17:31; Romans 1:4). A man who has been raised is a man who can come back.

The wrath to come. Modern readers flinch at wrath, often because they picture divine temper. That is not the biblical idea. God’s wrath is his settled, just opposition to evil, and a God who felt nothing about cruelty would not be good; we would not admire a judge who shrugged at atrocity. The wrath to come is God’s judgement on sin at the end (Romans 2:5; 5:9), when the accounts of history will finally be settled.

The tense is the comfort. Paul does not tell frightened, persecuted people that wrath is coming for them. Jesus delivers (rhyomai, rescues), and the participle is present. It works almost as a title, Jesus our Rescuer, the one whose rescue is already secured. The wrath is future; the deliverance is a fact now. They have been taken out already, by the one who absorbed it himself, bearing in his own body on the cross the judgement his people deserved.

Where Christians differ: wrath and the rapture. Some read deliverance from the wrath to come (here and 5:9) as a promise that believers will be removed from the earth in a secret rapture (from the Latin for being caught up, 4:17) before a seven-year tribulation. Many earnest, Bible-loving Christians hold this, reasoning that the tribulation is God’s wrath and his people are not destined for it. Verdict: The wrath to come is God’s final judgement on the ungodly at the last day (Romans 2:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). Believers are rescued from it through Christ’s death and resurrection. This does not promise escape from all suffering beforehand; the Thessalonians were already suffering (v. 6; 3:3). Christ will return once, visibly, to raise the dead, rescue his people and judge the world. There is no secret rapture. The reason: Paul describes one public coming, with a shout and a trumpet (4:16), and when he speaks of our being gathered to Christ he says that day will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear first (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3).

Why would a loving God have wrath at all? Because love that does not oppose evil is not love. A father who felt nothing when his child was abused would not be loving; he would be indifferent. God’s wrath is the resistance of his holiness and love to everything that destroys what he made. The wonder of the gospel is not that God has no wrath, but that he himself, in his Son, bore it for us, so that his justice and his mercy meet at the cross (Romans 3:25–26).

I still sin. Am I really safe from the wrath to come? Yes, if you are in Christ. Your rescue does not rest on how well you have done this week but on what Jesus did once for all and on his present work for you. The wrath your sins deserve fell on him; there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Your continuing sin should grieve you and drive you back to him, but it cannot reopen a case he has closed. He delivers, present tense: he is still doing it.

Does waiting for Jesus mean I should try to work out when he will come? No. Jesus said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), and Paul will say the day comes like a thief (5:2). Waiting means living ready, not calculating dates. It means holding this world loosely, serving faithfully where you are, and being glad, not afraid, at the thought of his coming, which is always near (Philippians 4:5).

A whole life in ten verses. Turned, serving, waiting: past, present and future, the whole Christian life inside ten verses, and Jesus at both ends of it, the one who was raised and the one who is coming.
