2.title: A Nursing Mother and a Urging Father
2.overview: After Paul’s hurried departure, someone was evidently saying he had been just another travelling religious salesman: a flatterer after money and fame who ran when it got hard. Paul answers by appealing to what the Thessalonians saw with their own eyes, from his arrival bruised from Philippi to his nights at a workbench. He thanks God that they received his message as God’s word, though it cost them persecution. Then his grief shows: he was “orphaned” from them, Satan blocked his return, yet they are his hope, joy and crown when the Lord Jesus comes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them how the mission began: bold preaching after mistreatment in Philippi, no flattery, greed or demand for honour, the gentleness of a mother, the hard work of a man paying his own way, and the urging of a father that they live worthily of the God who calls them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The minister as steward, not owner

The governing idea of the passage is in verse 4: entrusted with the gospel. A minister stands under the word, not over it; he is a steward, never an entrepreneur. And the God who approved him goes on testing his heart, so the question in every sermon and conversation is whose verdict he is working for.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The circuit Paul travelled was worked by professional lecturers who lived on their rhetoric, took what they could get, and moved on. So Paul answers with what could be checked: they had watched him arrive injured and preach anyway, and watched him at a leatherworker’s bench before dawn and after dark.

Now: Paul had the right to be supported and honoured and declined to press it. For anyone holding office, the question is almost never whether you have a right, but what you intend to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 2 is Paul’s defence of his ministry in Thessalonica. After his sudden departure, opponents seem to have said he was another travelling preacher, in it for money or fame, who abandoned his converts at the first sign of trouble. Paul reminds them what they saw: he preached boldly despite suffering, spoke to please God rather than people, used no flattery and sought no money, was gentle as a nursing mother, worked night and day to support himself, and exhorted them like a father (vv. 1–12). He thanks God that they received his message as the word of God and endured persecution as the Judean churches had (vv. 13–16). His absence was not his choice: Satan blocked the way, and they are his hope, joy and crown at Christ’s coming (vv. 17–20). Behind this portrait of a true pastor stands, at every turn, the Chief Shepherd whose likeness Paul bears.

The accusation behind the chapter. Something had been said about Paul in Thessalonica after he left, and you can hear its shape in what he denies: that he was a flatterer, after money, chasing a reputation, and that he ran when it got difficult. Travelling philosophers and religious salesmen worked that circuit constantly, and the easiest way to damage a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been another of them. So Paul keeps saying, you know: you were there. His defence is their own memory.

Not in vain. The word is kenos, empty, hollow. Paul means the whole enterprise had content and produced something, and the congregation reading the letter was the proof.

Shamefully treated at Philippi. In Philippi he and Silas had been stripped in the marketplace, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks (Acts 16:22–24), illegally, since they were Roman citizens. The word carries insult, not just injury. Thessalonica was the next city of any size, about a hundred miles down the road, and he arrived still marked.

Boldness in our God. He preached anyway. The verb (parrēsiazomai) is the freedom to speak openly and hide nothing. Note its source: in our God, not in his own nerve. This was borrowed courage, the opposite of the boast he is accused of, and the gospel he declared was God’s own news about his Son, not Paul’s scheme.

In the midst of much conflict. The word is agōn, the struggle in the arena: conflict going on while he spoke (Acts 17:5). Acts tells how it ended: a mob, a riot, and the believers getting him out of the city by night.

The cost is the credential. Here is the argument of the whole chapter in miniature. A man in it for money or applause does not walk from a flogging in one city into a riot in the next.

Shamefully treated, like his Lord. The word Paul uses for Philippi (hybrizō) is the word Jesus used of his own coming suffering: the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles and mocked and shamefully treated and spat upon (Luke 18:32). Paul was walking where his Lord had walked first, and the apostles had already learned to rejoice that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). That is why the shame did not silence him. A man who preaches a Christ who was insulted and beaten does not find insult a reason to stop; he finds it a strange confirmation that he belongs to the one he preaches.

Where does boldness come from, if I am naturally timid? From God, not from temperament. Paul did not say he was brave; he said he had boldness in our God. Courage of this kind grows from being sure of the message, sure of the God who sends it, and more concerned for the hearer than for yourself. Pray for it, as the apostles did (Acts 4:29). Then take the next small step: one honest sentence about Christ to one person. Boldness is usually given in the act of obeying, not beforehand.

Should I keep speaking about Christ after I have been hurt for it? Usually yes, though wisdom matters. Paul moved on from Philippi but did not go silent; he preached in the next city. Sometimes the right thing is to leave a hostile place, as he did more than once. But being hurt is not a sign God has withdrawn his call. Bring the wound to him, let others in the church care for you, and then speak again when he opens the door.
verseByVerse.note: At Philippi Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed just before they came to Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Error, impurity, deceit. The appeal (paraklēsis) is Paul’s preaching, and the three denials cover three ways a ministry goes wrong. Error (planē) is about the message: a man may be sincere and simply wrong. Impurity (akatharsia) is about motive, and the word often carried a sexual edge; a travelling teacher with access to households was a known hazard. Deceit (dolos) is about method: cunning trickery, the angler’s art of hiding the hook. Any one of them is enough to ruin a ministry that is sound in the other two.

Approved by God. Approved (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word for testing metal and finding it genuine. Paul uses it twice in one sentence: he has been tested and passed by the God who tests hearts, and the examination is continuous. So Paul did not appoint himself. God examined him, found him fit and gave him the gospel to carry (1 Timothy 1:12), and that same God goes on examining his heart every time he speaks.

Entrusted. To be entrusted is to be trusted with something that belongs to another, as a steward is given his master’s goods (1 Corinthians 4:1–2). It is not Paul’s gospel; he is a courier carrying something that belongs to someone else, and a courier does not get to edit the parcel.

To please God who tests our hearts. Everything turns on this sentence (Jeremiah 11:20; Psalm 139:23; Galatians 1:10). It is not indifference to people; Paul is about to describe how tenderly he treated them. It is a question of which verdict he works for. And the two audiences pull constantly in opposite directions: one can be pleased by softening what is hard, and the other sees the heart while you do it.

The one who always pleased the Father. Paul’s rule was first his Master’s life. Jesus said of the Father, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), and Paul says of him that Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3). He slipped away from the crowd that wanted to make him king by force (John 6:15), and he refused the devil’s offer of the kingdoms without a cross (Matthew 4:8–10). Every faithful courier of the gospel is copying that one life, and every one of them falls short of it.

What does it look like to please people rather than God? It looks like leaving out the parts of the truth that would cost you: never mentioning repentance or judgement, agreeing with whoever is in the room, staying silent when a friend is going wrong, shaping what you say by what will be liked. It is often driven by fear dressed up as kindness. Pleasing God does not mean being harsh; Paul was gentle. It means saying the true thing in a loving way, and letting God judge the result.

On a Tuesday. Every preacher, teacher and parent knows the moment when the true thing and the popular thing part company. Before a hard conversation this week, with a child, a colleague, a friend, ask yourself whose approval you are working for. Then pray the psalmist’s prayer, that God would search you and know your heart, and go in to say what is true and kind.

For worship. The gospel is God’s treasure, not ours, and he has been pleased to put it into clay jars, carrying a light that is not their own (2 Corinthians 4:7). He searches every heart and is never deceived, and still he entrusts. The God who tests hearts found in his Son a heart that passed every test, and he has made that Son our righteousness, so that tried and failing servants stand approved in him. The one audience worth pleasing is the one who has already made us acceptable in the Beloved.

verseByVerse.quote: For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Words of flattery. Flattery is not kindness or encouragement. It is saying what a person wants to hear in order to get something from them: praise with a hook in it. The ancient moralists despised the flatterer as a manipulator wearing a friend’s face. For this charge Paul appeals to their memory: you heard what I actually said.

A pretext for greed. Here the evidence changes. A pretext (prophasis) is a cover story: ministry as a front for making money. But greed is a motive, and motives are invisible, so Paul calls the one witness who can see them.

Glory from people. This is subtler than money and more common among religious people: a man can be scrupulous about cash and still feed on being admired. And not from you or from others means he was not building a reputation to spend somewhere else.

We could have made demands. Literally, though we could have been a weight: they could have stood on their dignity and asked for support. Paul defends that right vigorously elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:4–14) before saying he has never used it. This is a man with every entitlement declining to press it.

The mind of Christ. This is exactly the mind Paul describes in the passage often thought to be an early Christian hymn: one who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6). The question in ministry, as in every relationship where one person holds power, is almost never whether you have a right. Usually you do. It is what you intend to do with the right you have.

How can I tell encouragement from flattery in myself? Ask three questions. Is it true? Flattery exaggerates or invents. Is it for their good or for mine? Flattery wants something back: favour, a contract, to be liked. Would I say it behind their back too? Flattery is spoken to the face only. Encouragement names real grace in someone, specifically, and then gives God the credit. Practise that kind freely; the church is starved of it.

Is it wrong to want to be appreciated? No. Paul longed to be loved by his churches, and it is human to be glad when your work is valued. What is wrong is making people’s praise the reason you serve, so that you sulk when it is missing or shape the work to get it. Do the work for God, receive thanks gratefully when it comes, and pass the glory on.

verseByVerse.quote: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we were gentle among you. Having said what he was not, Paul says what he was, and reaches for an image no one would have expected from him. Gentle (ēpioi) is the opposite of domineering. Paul, the man of iron in Galatians, is soft with these new believers.

The textual question. The Greek manuscripts divide between ēpioi, gentle, and nēpioi, infants, one letter apart, as the ESV footnote notes; in ancient copies without word spacing the preceding word ends in that same letter, so the confusion is easy. Several of the earliest manuscripts read infants, and some modern Bibles (the NIV, for one) follow them, while others judge gentle the better fit. If it is infants, Paul says he became like a small child among them, without airs or demands, before shifting to the nursing mother. Either reading tells against the charge of self-importance, and the ESV’s gentle gives the smoother sense.

Like a nursing mother. The phrase her own is doing real work: not a hired wet nurse minding somebody else’s baby, but a mother feeding her own child. The verb (thalpō) means to cherish, to keep warm, and is used of a bird brooding over her eggs: the most ordinary and most costly self-giving there is, at night, unseen, with no audience.

Affectionately desirous. The word homeiromai appears nowhere else in the New Testament and is known elsewhere chiefly from a gravestone where grieving parents use it, it seems, of a lost child: the ache of wanting someone you cannot reach. That is what Paul felt for a church he had known for a month or so.

Our own selves. This sentence defines pastoral work. The word for selves (psychai) means lives: time, energy, hearts. It is possible to deliver the message accurately and withhold the man, and much religious professionalism is exactly that: correct content, carefully rationed distance. Gospel ministry is life on life.

Very dear to us. That is the reason, and it is not a strategy. Love makes a person hand over more than was required, and anyone served by someone who plainly liked them, rather than someone discharging a duty, knows the difference.

More than his life shared. Paul’s readiness to give his own self is a small copy of something far larger. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), the same word for life that Paul uses here. But Paul offered his time, strength and heart; Christ, in Paul’s own words, loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and at his table he says, this is my body, given for you (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). The gospel is not a message Christ sends while keeping his distance. The messenger is the message, and he gave himself with it.

Is it right for a male apostle to call himself a nursing mother? Yes, and it is beautiful. Scripture uses mother imagery for God’s own tenderness (Isaiah 49:15; 66:13), and Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks (Matthew 23:37). Paul uses it to show the tenderness every true shepherd needs, not to blur the callings of men and women. Leaders in the church, who are to be qualified men, are not meant to be cold. (This commentary reads 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:1–7 as giving the office of elder to qualified men; many faithful Christians read those passages differently, and the point here does not depend on it: no shepherd, of any view, is meant to be cold.) Their authority is the self-giving care of a mother at night as well as the steady formation of a father.

I am not a pastor. How do I share my life as well as the gospel? Open your ordinary life to people. Invite someone into your home, not just to an event. Let them see you pray, fail, apologise and keep trusting. Spend time with a younger believer, a lonely neighbour or a new member over months, not minutes. Share meals, lifts, worries. Most people are not won or grown by programmes but by being loved by a Christian who lets them close enough to see Christ at work.

For worship. Before Paul was a nursing mother to Thessalonica, God was one to Israel: can a woman forget her nursing child? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you, says the LORD (Isaiah 49:15). He has kept that word in his Son. The God who would not forget his children came and fed them with himself, the living bread given for the life of the world (John 6:51), and he goes on feeding them, night after night, with no audience and little thanks, until they are grown.

verseByVerse.quote: For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Labour and toil. This is the hardest evidence in the chapter. Kopos is labour to the point of exhaustion; mochthos is hardship, the grind. Paul is not describing a trade he enjoyed. He is describing being tired.

We worked night and day. The trade was probably the tentmaking or leatherworking Luke mentions in Corinth (Acts 18:3; 20:34): heavy, unglamorous work with awl and knife, the kind of labour gentlemen despised. Night and day means he was at the bench before dawn and after dark, with the preaching fitted around it. Philippi also sent him gifts while he was in Thessalonica (Philippians 4:16), and even with that help he worked.

Not a weight on anyone. The word for burden means a weight laid on someone. He had just told them (v. 6) that he could have made demands as an apostle. Here is what he did instead. The right existed, and he paid out of his own pocket rather than use it, so that he would not burden a poor young church or give any ground to the charge of greed.

The answer without argument. A man running a religious racket does not work a double shift to avoid taking money from his converts. The Thessalonians would have seen him come to the meeting with his hands still rough from the workshop.

Free of charge. The work served the word. The bench was never the point; the gospel was. Paul’s hands earned bread so that his mouth could give away the bread of life without a price attached. He tells the Corinthians the same: he preached God’s gospel to them free of charge (2 Corinthians 11:7). The reason runs to the heart of the message. The gospel is free because it has been paid for. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). A preacher who sold that news would misrepresent it, and a preacher who worked a double shift to give it away was preaching it with his hands.

Should my church pay its pastor, then? Yes, normally. Scripture says the labourer deserves his wages and that those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:17–18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). A paid pastor is not less spiritual than a self-supporting one. Paul’s choice in Thessalonica was a freedom he used for a reason, not a rule for every church. Churches should support their ministers generously, and ministers should guard their hearts against loving money.

Does ordinary work matter to God? Very much. Paul did not see the workshop as a distraction from real ministry. It was part of his witness. Your job, done honestly and well, is service to Christ (Colossians 3:23–24), provides for your family and the needy (4:11–12; Ephesians 4:28), and gives you daily contact with people who need the gospel. You do not have to leave work to serve God. You serve him there.
verseByVerse.note: Paul supported himself by his trade — he was a tentmaker.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses, and God also. Both courts again: the one that saw his conduct and the one that sees his heart. Holy is devoted to God, righteous is just toward people, blameless is with nothing anyone could lay a charge on. Paul is not claiming sinlessness, but that no accusation would stick, which is testable. And he calls God as a witness, not only the church. He lived knowing that the holy God watched what he did in the workshop and in private houses as closely as what he said in the synagogue. That is what kept him clean, and it is a sobering thought for anyone who serves in public: God sees the hours no one else sees.

Like a father. The second family image, deliberately paired. The nursing mother (v. 7) carried warmth and self-giving; the father in the ancient household carried formation, responsibility for teaching and training, for what the child became.

Exhorted, encouraged, charged. Exhorted (parakaleō): coming alongside to urge. Encouraged (paramytheomai): putting heart into someone. Charged (martyromai): a solemn testifying that puts someone under obligation. Warmth and weight together. A father who only encourages raises children who cannot stand; one who only charges raises children who leave.

Each one of you. In perhaps a month, while also working night and day at a bench, Paul dealt with these people individually, as he later did house to house in Ephesus (Acts 20:20). He did not preach at a crowd and move on. He knew them one at a time.

To walk in a manner worthy of God. Worthy is not a standard they must reach to earn something. It is a matching: conduct that fits who God is and what has happened to you, as a uniform fits the service you are in.

Who calls you into his own kingdom and glory. The calling is present and ongoing: God called them once and is calling them still, toward the kingdom and glory that are their destination. The walk is shaped by where it ends. That is Paul’s whole method of motivating people: not behave, or else, but this is where you are going; live like someone going there.

The glory is Christ’s. What is the glory God calls them into? Paul answers in his second letter: they were called through the gospel to obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:14), and those he called he also glorified, conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29–30). So the walk worthy of God has a face: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked (1 John 2:6). A Christian is not straining after an abstract standard but growing into the likeness of the Lord whose glory he will share.

What is God’s kingdom and glory, and am I in it now? God’s kingdom is his saving rule through Christ. It has already begun: believers have been transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). But its full glory is still to come when Christ returns, and that glory is a share in God’s own splendour, the life of the age to come in his presence (Romans 8:18; 2 Thessalonians 2:14). So you are in it now, and you are being called further into it. You are a citizen already, walking toward the capital.

What does living worthy of God look like on an ordinary day? It looks like the life Paul describes in chapters 4 and 5: sexual purity, brotherly love, quiet honest work, hope at the graveside, alertness, respect for leaders, patience with the weak, joy, prayer and thanksgiving. It is not a special religious mood but ordinary life brought under the King. When you are unsure what to do, ask what fits a child of God who is on the way to his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:13–16 – How They Received the Word — and What It Cost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God that they received the message as what it truly is, God’s word, now at work in them. They have suffered from their own people as the churches in Judea did, and Paul speaks severely of those who killed the Lord and were trying to stop the gospel reaching the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Scripture as God’s own speech

Verse 13 is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of what Scripture is. Its authority does not wait on our verdict; but only those who hear it as God’s word find it working in them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 15–16 have been misused across the centuries. Paul, himself a Jew, names a target by its actions, in the insider language of covenant rebuke.

Now: The wrath of verse 16 must be read beside 1:10, where wrath is what Jesus delivers people from, Paul himself included. A sober warning is never a licence for contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks a second time. Paul’s thanks now is for how they took what they heard.

In the flow. Verses 1 to 12 defended the messengers; verse 13 turns to the message, and shows why the defence mattered. If Paul had been a fraud, his word would be suspect too. But the Thessalonians had heard God in it, and it was working in them. That takes the reader back to the gospel that came with power and full conviction (1:5), and it prepares verses 14–16: the clearest proof that the word was at work is that they kept believing when it cost them their neighbours.

Received and accepted. They received it (paralambanō), the ordinary term for taking delivery of something; then they accepted it (dechomai), the word for welcoming a guest into your house. The first is hearing; the second is embracing. Plenty of people do the first every Sunday and never do the second.

What it really is. They had heard it from a leatherworker with marks on his back, in a synagogue and a private house, in a city full of competing lecturers. Nothing about the delivery compelled the verdict, yet they concluded they were being addressed by God, and Paul says they were right: what it really is.

The decision every hearer makes. Every hearer of Scripture makes it, usually without noticing. If the Bible is a valuable human document, you weigh it, keep what persuades you, and remain the judge. If it is the word of God, the relation reverses and it reads you. There is no third option where it is God’s word and you still hold the editorial pencil.

At work in you. The verb is energeō, the root of our word energy, and it is present and continuous: the word is working in them now, while Paul writes (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 55:11). God’s word is not dead letters but living power.

Two kinds of hearing. Paul is describing not two kinds of Bible but two kinds of hearing, and the second produced the work of faith, the labour of love and the endurance he thanked God for at the start of the letter (1:3).

Hearing the Lord in his messengers. Jesus had told his apostles that this would happen: the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me (Luke 10:16). The Thessalonians heard a leatherworker and met the risen Christ, because the apostolic word is the word of Christ (Colossians 3:16), and his sheep hear their shepherd’s voice in it (John 10:27). That is what accepting it as the word of God means in practice. You are not admiring Paul’s argument; you are being addressed by the Lord himself, and answering him.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture the word of God? Some say the Bible contains or becomes the word of God, or is merely human testimony. Verdict: The apostles’ message, now written in Scripture, is what it really is: the word of God, not merely the words of men, though spoken through men. Scripture is God-breathed and authoritative in all it affirms (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession confess (Westminster 1.4; 1689 1.4). Its authority does not depend on human acceptance; it is God’s word whether received or not, and it works in those who believe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every preacher’s words are God’s word. Only as preaching faithfully conveys Scripture does it carry God’s authority.

How can a book written by men be God’s word? Because God spoke through them, not around them. He used their personalities, languages, research and circumstances, and so superintended their writing that what they wrote is exactly what he intended to say (2 Peter 1:21). Paul wrote as Paul, with his own warmth and style, and yet the Thessalonians were right to hear God. The human and divine are not rivals in Scripture any more than in the person of Christ, who is fully human and fully God.

Is it not circular to believe the Bible is God’s word because the Bible says so? Every final authority has to vouch for itself, or it would not be final. A person who trusts reason alone can only defend reason by reasoning. The Thessalonians were not argued into faith by a clever proof. They heard the word, and it did what only God’s word does: it showed them their idols, set Christ before them, and changed them. The Spirit himself convinces people that Scripture is God’s word as they hear it (Westminster 1.5; 1689 1.5), and he does it through its message, not apart from it. There are good reasons too: the resurrection of Jesus, and Jesus’ own trust in the Scriptures (John 10:35). But in the end God’s word is believed the way the sun is seen: by its own light. That cannot be proved like a sum, and an honest doubter is not a fool for asking; the invitation is the one the Thessalonians accepted, to hear it and see what it does.

How do I receive the word as God’s word when I read it? Come expecting God to speak, not merely to gather information. Pray before you read, asking him to open your eyes. Read to obey, not just to understand: ask what it shows you of God and Christ, what it promises, what it commands, and what you must believe or change. When it contradicts you, let it win. And keep coming back. The word works over time, like seed, not usually like lightning.

What about new revelations or prophecies today? The word that works in believers is the apostolic word, now complete in Scripture. The canon is closed: God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the apostles’ teaching is the foundation the church is built on (Ephesians 2:20). Impressions and promptings must always be tested by Scripture and never placed beside it. Everything we need for life and godliness is already given there.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imitators of the churches in Judea. In chapter 1 they imitated Paul and the Lord; here, congregations nearly a thousand miles away that they had never met. The proof that the word was at work in them: they endured persecution as the first churches had.

Your own countrymen. Paul matches the detail exactly. The Judean believers were opposed by fellow Jews (Acts 8:1–3; 12:1–3); the Thessalonian believers by fellow Thessalonians, stirred up by some of the synagogue (Acts 17:5–9). In each case the opposition came from the neighbours, which hurts most and costs most, because it is the loss of your own people.

What that meant in that city. These were Gentiles who had walked out of the guild dinners, household shrines and civic festivals, the whole social fabric. The pressure came from employers, families, and men they had drunk with all their lives.

Joining a line. A young church under attack asks in the middle of the night whether something has gone wrong. Paul’s answer is that they have joined a line: the same thing is happening to the oldest churches, planted where Jesus himself walked. Their suffering is not evidence that they took a wrong turn. It is evidence that they are on the road.

The road their Lord walked first. The line goes back further than Judea. Those churches were in Christ Jesus, and their suffering was his before it was theirs. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11); even his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). And he told his disciples to expect the same: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). So when the Thessalonians lost their neighbours for his sake, they were not on an unmarked path. They were walking in his footprints, and those footprints lead through a cross to an empty tomb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution proves a church true. Plenty of people are disliked for being disagreeable. But faithful churches should expect it (2 Timothy 3:12), and opposition is not proof of failure either, which is what the frightened heart assumes at three in the morning.

My own family opposes my faith. What should I do? You are in good company: Jesus said a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36), and the Thessalonians suffered from their own people. Stay loving, respectful and patient. Honour your parents and serve your family in every way that does not require disobeying Christ. Do not argue constantly; let your life speak, and speak when asked. Keep bringing them to God in prayer. Find support in your church family. And where there is any threat of harm, seek help and safety; enduring hostility is not the same as tolerating abuse.

Why does it help to know others suffer the same? Because suffering isolates and lies. It says you are alone, and that it means God has abandoned you. Knowing that Christians across the world and down the centuries have walked this road answers both lies. You belong to a family that has always suffered and always been kept. That is why it is right to pray for and learn about the persecuted church today: they strengthen us, and we can strengthen them.

For worship. When Saul of Tarsus was dragging believers out of their houses, the risen Lord stopped him on the road and asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The Head feels every blow that lands on his body. Not one believer pushed out of a guild in Thessalonica, or out of a family anywhere, suffers out of his sight or out of his heart; he counts their wounds as his own. And the voice that asked that question turned the persecutor into a brother. The Head who bled for his body will never abandon it.

verseByVerse.quote: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hardest passage in the letter. This passage has been misused across the centuries to justify appalling things, so it must be read carefully and its limits stated plainly.

Who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets. Start with who is speaking. Paul is himself a Jew, a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), who insists in Romans that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean what Romans denies. Nor is he condemning a race. His target is specific and he names their actions: the leaders who rejected Christ and handed him over, following a long pattern of killing the prophets (Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:52).

The language of covenant rebuke. The charge sheet is drawn from Israel’s own Scriptures. The prophets said harder things about their nation’s leaders than Paul does here, and Jesus lamented over Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37). This is the internal language of covenant rebuke, spoken by an insider, which is exactly what it stops being when outsiders pick it up as a weapon.

And drove us out. From Thessalonica and then from Beroea (Acts 17:5–10, 13). Paul is not recalling ancient history; he is describing what had happened to him a few months earlier.

Oppose all mankind. Oppose all mankind sounds sweeping, but it is aimed at one thing: obstructing the gospel from going to the nations. To stand in the way of the only message that saves is to act against humanity as such. It is a charge about the mission, not about race or character.

Fill up the measure. The picture is of a cup being filled. As God waited until the sin of the Amorites was complete (Genesis 15:16), and as Jesus told the leaders of his day to fill up the measure of their fathers (Matthew 23:32), so these opponents were filling up their sins to the point of judgement. God’s patience is long, and it has an end.

Wrath has come. The verb is past: already come. Paul most likely means that judgement is so certain, so visibly set in motion, that it can be spoken of as arrived, the prophetic past tense; within twenty years Jerusalem and the temple would fall (AD 70). At last may also mean fully, or to the end.

Did Paul write these verses? Some scholars think vv. 13–16 were added by a later writer, because they sound so harsh and seem to look back on the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. But no manuscript lacks them, and they fit Paul’s own experience of being driven out by Jewish opponents (Acts 17:5, 13). Nor are they a verdict on the Jewish people: Paul himself was a Jew who longed for their salvation (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1).

Where Christians differ: is this anti-Jewish? Some say this passage is anti-Semitic, or that it was not written by Paul. Verdict: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, not of the Jewish people as a whole. He loved his people deeply and longed for their salvation (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1), and many of the first believers were Jews. His language echoes Jesus and the prophets, who spoke similarly to Israel. Christians must never use this passage to justify hatred of Jews, which is a terrible sin that has stained church history.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all Jews are under wrath, or that Jews alone killed Jesus. Gentiles shared in it (Acts 4:27), and our sins put him there.

The passage ends where the letter began. Wrath is what Jesus delivers people from (1:10), including Paul, once a persecutor hindering the gospel, and rescued. Opposition to the gospel places any people, Jew or Gentile, under the wrath the gospel exists to save them from, and the same gospel stands open to them. And consider who the opponents were: not irreligious men but zealous ones, as Paul himself had been (Galatians 1:13–14). Religion used to earn a standing with God can make a person the fiercest enemy of grace, because grace tells him his record counts for nothing. A sober warning is not a licence for contempt, and anyone who has used this passage for contempt has read the man who wrote Romans 11 exactly backwards.

Does this passage settle what God will do with Israel in the future? No. It describes the judgement on those who were rejecting Christ and blocking the gospel in Paul’s own day. Whether Romans 11 promises a large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end is a question on which faithful Reformed Christians differ, and this verse does not decide it. What every view agrees on is that Jewish people, like everyone, are saved only through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that the church should long and pray for their salvation, as Paul did.

How should I treat people who oppose the gospel? Pray for them, love them, and keep telling them the truth. Paul could describe his opponents in the strongest terms and still spend his life preaching to them. Remember that you yourself were once an enemy of God (Romans 5:10), and that the fiercest opponent of the church in that generation became its greatest missionary. Leave judgement to God, and never return hatred for hatred.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was killed by the hands of lawless men, Jew and Gentile together, and our sins were in their hands. And from the cross he prayed, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34, a prayer missing from some early manuscripts but widely received as genuine). The wrath that opposition to God deserves fell on him, so that persecutors like Saul of Tarsus could be made apostles, and enemies like us could be made sons. Glory to the Messiah of Israel and the Saviour of the nations.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, as he had once done — not of every Jewish person.

parallels.desc: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

verseByVerse.ref: 2:17–20 – Orphaned From Them, and What He Expects to Hold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Torn away from them, Paul tried more than once to return, but Satan blocked the way. They are his hope, joy and crown at the Lord’s coming.
verseByVerse.theology:
The coming, and the pastor’s wreath

The reward of pastoral work is not the admiration of the present age but the sight, on that day, of people standing before Jesus because the gospel was faithfully preached and patiently tended.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enemy who blocked Paul’s road did not win: Timothy went in his place, and this letter exists because Paul could not come.

Now: On the last day, is what you expect to hold up a record of what you achieved, or people who are standing there because of it?

verseByVerse.quote: But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Torn away. Torn away is aporphanisthentes, built on the word for orphan. Having called himself their mother and their father, Paul is now the bereaved one, an extraordinary thing for a grown man to write about a congregation he had known for weeks. And his departure was forced (Acts 17:10); he did not abandon them, as his critics said.

In person not in heart. Two qualifications keep the grief from being despair. For a short time: the separation is temporary, whatever it feels like. And in person not in heart, literally in face, not in heart: the distance is physical only.

The more eagerly. Being torn away made him try harder rather than settle into resignation. Opponents said he did not care; he cared intensely.

I, Paul, again and again. The sentence breaks apart under the feeling: he interrupts his own plural to sign his name. He wants them to know that he tried, personally and repeatedly.

Satan hindered us. The verb (enkoptō) means to block or hinder, and is often pictured as breaking up a road to stop an army. Paul does not tell us the mechanism: it may have been the bond the authorities took from Jason (Acts 17:9), which made his return dangerous for his hosts, or illness, or hostility elsewhere. What matters is how he read it: not as bad luck or as God saying no, but as the work of an enemy with an interest in keeping a young church away from its teacher.

Can Satan thwart God’s plans? He can hinder our plans, but only within God’s permission, as with Job (Job 1–2) and Paul’s thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7). Paul was kept from Thessalonica, and God used even that: this letter was written because he could not come. God’s purposes are never defeated.

Where Christians differ: Satan’s power over circumstances. Some blame Satan for every difficulty; others ignore him. Verdict: Satan is real and does oppose God’s work, sometimes through circumstances (Job 1–2; 2 Corinthians 12:7). But he acts only within the limits God permits, and God overrules even his opposition for good (Romans 8:28). Elsewhere Luke tells us the Spirit prevented Paul from going somewhere (Acts 16:6–7). Discernment is needed, and in every case we trust God’s sovereign providence, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 5.4; 1689 5.4).

Hold it with care, in both directions. Not everything that goes wrong is a demonic assault, and a Christian who reads every delay that way will be exhausted and superstitious. But Paul did not think his frustrations merely administrative. And he never says Satan won. Timothy went instead (3:2), and the letter you are reading was written because Paul could not come, which is not a bad accounting of who was hindered in the end.

Not left as orphans. Paul says he was orphaned from them, and the word recalls a promise. On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples, I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you (John 14:18), and he spoke of the Spirit who would be with them for ever. That is why the broken road was not a disaster for Thessalonica. The apostle could be kept away; the Lord could not. Paul felt bereaved, but the church was not abandoned, because the risen Christ was present among them by his Spirit while their teacher was stuck far to the south.

How can I tell whether Satan is hindering me or God is closing a door? Often you cannot tell, and you do not need to. Paul read one blocked road as Satan’s work and another as the Spirit’s, and in both he did the same thing: trusted God, kept praying, and did what he could do. Ask whether the plan was clearly good and in line with Scripture. Keep seeking it by lawful means. If the door stays shut, accept it from God’s hand, and look for the other way he may be opening, as Timothy went when Paul could not.

Is it right to grieve over separation from Christian friends? Yes. Paul felt it like bereavement and was not ashamed to say so. Love for brothers and sisters in Christ is meant to be strong enough to hurt when we are parted. Bring the ache to God, keep in touch as you can (Paul wrote a letter and sent a friend), and remember that every separation between believers is for a short time. There is a day of reunion that no road-block can stop.

verseByVerse.quote: For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Paul has been defending himself against the charge of chasing glory (v. 6). Now, at the end of the chapter, he says what he is actually after, and the answer is the people he is writing to. He asks it as a question and answers it himself, and the effect is warmer than a statement would have been.

Crown. The stephanos is not the royal diadem but the victor’s wreath at the games, and in a city like Thessalonica a wreath could also be presented when a king or emperor visited. That is the scene Paul describes.

At his coming. The word is parousia, used here for the first time in this letter of Christ’s return. In ordinary Greek it meant arrival, especially the state visit of a sovereign to one of his cities, when the citizens streamed out to meet him on the road and escorted him in. Paul applies that civic vocabulary to the return of Jesus.

Is it not you? So the picture is this: the King arrives, and Paul is standing there, and what he has to show is not a record of his labours but a group of people. Their being there is the wreath.

Our glory and joy. Said plainly, and in the present tense: not only will be, on that day, but are, now, while he is separated from them and unable to get back (Philippians 4:1).

The accusation settled. This settles the accusation of the chapter better than any denial. A man seeking glory from people uses them and moves on. Paul’s glory is them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s salvation depended on them. His hope of eternal life rested on Christ alone. It means they will be the joy and fruit of his labour.

Will Christians receive rewards in heaven? Yes. Scripture speaks of crowns and rewards given by Christ (1 Corinthians 3:12–14; 2 Timothy 4:8), not to earn salvation, which is a free gift, but as the Father’s gracious recognition of what his children did by his grace. Even our rewards are gifts: God crowns his own works in us. And the greatest reward is not a thing but a joy: to see Christ, and to see with him the people we loved and served for his sake.

Will we recognise one another when Christ comes? Paul expects to: he looks forward to standing with these very people before the Lord. Scripture never suggests we lose who we are in glory. The disciples recognised Moses and Elijah, and the risen Jesus was known by his friends. Paul will build on this in chapter 4, where the dead and the living are brought together to meet the Lord. Christian love is not ended by death; it is gathered up into the joy of his coming.

For worship. The King is coming, and his people will go out to meet him. On that day every faithful labour will be seen for what it was, and every saint will stand in his presence, the joy of those who loved them and the reward of the Saviour who died for them. For Christ, too, has a joy set before him: the people his Father gave him, brought home. Glory to the coming King.
