3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview: Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution. So he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to strengthen them. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding. Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord,” and the chapter ends in a prayer that looks ahead to the rest of the letter: love that overflows, and hearts blameless in holiness when Jesus comes.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, so that no one would be shaken by the suffering he had warned them to expect, and for fear that the tempter had undone his work.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as appointment, not accident

Suffering for the gospel is not something that slipped past God’s attention; it is a placement. God governs all things, his people’s afflictions included, and he makes such suffering purposeful, producing endurance, character and hope (Romans 5:3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v. 3).

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and leaving it out is no kindness (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 3 shows a pastor’s heart in anxiety and relief. Unable to bear not knowing how the young church was standing under persecution, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, fearing that the tempter had shaken them (vv. 1–5). Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love and their longing to see him, and Paul came alive again: now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord (vv. 6–8). He overflows with thanks and prays night and day to see them and supply what is lacking in their faith (vv. 9–10). He ends in prayer: that God would open the way, make their love overflow, and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his saints (vv. 11–13). Behind the human drama stands the God who keeps his people when their pastor cannot reach them.

Could bear it no longer. The verb is stegō, to bear or hold in, a word that could also describe a roof keeping out the rain. Paul had been holding in his anxiety, and he could hold it no longer. He says it twice in five verses (vv. 1, 5): a man telling you what the months had been like.

Left behind at Athens alone. The cost is easy to miss. Athens was where Paul’s spirit was provoked by a city full of idols, where he was mocked at the Areopagus for mentioning resurrection, and where he made few converts (Acts 17:15–34): some of the thinnest ground he ever worked. In that city he gave away his companion. The word for left behind (kataleipō) is used elsewhere of being abandoned, and alone carries its weight at the end of the clause. Paul, whose letters are full of names, chose isolation because a frightened congregation needed someone more than he did: sharing not only the gospel but his own self (2:8), at an actual price.

God’s coworker. Not his assistant: God’s coworker, a startling title for a young man. Some manuscripts read God’s servant, as the ESV notes, probably because copyists found the bolder title surprising. Steadying a church is God’s work, and the person doing it works alongside God.

To establish and exhort. To establish (stērizō) is to make firm, as you might prop up a leaning wall; to exhort (parakaleō) is to come alongside and urge. Both are about stability rather than growth: when a church is under attack, the first task is to keep it standing.

The Lord who establishes. Timothy was sent to do what, in the end, only the Lord can do. Paul prays that God would establish their hearts (3:13), and writes in his second letter that the Lord is faithful; he will establish you and guard you against the evil one (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Timothy’s visit was the means. The one holding up the leaning wall was the risen Christ, who said, I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). That is why Timothy can be called God’s coworker without exaggeration: he worked on a building whose Builder never leaves the site.

If God keeps his people, why was Paul so anxious? Because God keeps his people through means, and Paul was one of the means. Trusting God’s sovereignty never made Paul passive; it made him pray and send. His anxiety was the anxiety of love, not of unbelief, and he did with it what love should do: he acted, and he brought it to God. Your concern for a struggling believer is not a lack of faith. It may be God’s way of moving you to be the help he intends.

What does following up a new believer actually involve? What Timothy did: going to them, strengthening their grasp of the truth, encouraging them to keep going, and preparing them for trouble. In practice that means meeting regularly, reading the Bible together, answering questions, praying with them, introducing them to other believers, and noticing when they go quiet. It does not require a title. It requires time, patience and love, and it is some of the most fruitful work in the church.

For worship. Paul chose to be alone in Athens so that a frightened church would not be alone. Long before, the Son of God let every friend leave him so that his people would never be left: you will leave me alone, he told them, yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me (John 16:32). Because he was deserted, not one of his own is ever abandoned. He props up leaning walls and steadies trembling hearts, and he lets ordinary believers share the work as his coworkers, an honour no apostle ever earned.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That no one be moved. The verb is sainō. Its oldest sense was a dog wagging its tail, and so to fawn or coax; by Paul’s day it could also mean to unsettle or disturb, and most translations take it that way. Either way, Paul’s worry is not only that persecution would smash them, but that under sustained pressure they might be gently talked out of it, coaxed back to the life they had left or into compromise to escape the pressure.

How faith is usually lost. Not in a moment of dramatic renunciation, but by erosion: the family who keep asking, the invitation it is easier to accept, the guild dinner it costs too much to refuse. A wagging tail, not a battering ram.

Destined for this. The verb is keimetha: we are laid, set in place, appointed, the verb Paul used of himself in prison, set there for the defence of the gospel (Philippians 1:16), and of the foundation already laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). Affliction did not slip past God’s attention. It is a placement (Acts 14:22; John 16:33; 2 Timothy 3:12).

The pastoral logic. What steadies a shaken believer is not being told the trouble will stop, but being told it is not a mistake. If suffering means the plan has gone wrong, every hard week is evidence against the faith; if suffering is where God has laid you, the hard week proves only that you are where he put you. Knowing this in advance protects from shock.

Appointed first for Christ. The placement began with Christ. On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord asked, was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). His suffering was not an accident God repaired afterwards; it was the appointed road, and glory lay at its end. What was appointed for the Head is appointed for his body: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). What does that mean under pressure? The trouble is not a sign you have left Christ’s path. It is evidence that you are on it, and his path ends in glory.

Does destined for this apply to all suffering, or only persecution? Paul’s immediate subject is suffering for the gospel, the pressure that comes because you belong to Christ. But the principle reaches further: nothing comes to God’s children by accident, whether illness, loss or disappointment, and he works all of it for their good (Romans 8:28). That does not make every hardship good in itself, nor does it mean you must not seek relief. Pray for healing, seek justice, take the medicine. But you can do so knowing that you are where your Father has placed you, and that he has not lost track of you.

Is it wrong to try to avoid persecution? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul left Thessalonica and Damascus by night. What is wrong is avoiding it by denying Christ or compromising obedience. You may leave, keep a low profile in some settings, or use the law’s protection, as Paul used his citizenship. You may not lie about him, worship what he forbids, or abandon his people to save yourself.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the places where you are being gently coaxed away from Christ: not attacked, just nudged. The joke you laugh along with, the habit you have quietly resumed, the conviction you no longer mention. Name it before God, who forgives it and does not let go of you, and stand where he has placed you.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We kept telling you beforehand. The tense is continuous. With a few weeks and an enormous amount he might have taught, Paul put this high on the list: this will cost you. He did not win them with an easier offer and explain the terms later. Honest evangelism counts the cost (Luke 14:28).

Just as it has come to pass. The warning was verified by events, and that was itself pastoral. A church told the truth in advance meets hardship saying, he said this would happen; a church promised an easy road meets the same hardship asking whether the whole thing was false.

I sent. Now the plural becomes singular. Paul admits his own fear, and he is not embarrassed by it.

The tempter. The tempter is the title used of Satan in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3), where the tactic was not violence but suggestion. Paul has already named him as the one who cut the road (2:18). He sees a strategy: block the teacher, then work on the church, using suffering to tempt believers to give up.

The tempter has met his match. Paul feared the tempter because he knew his methods, and he knew who had beaten him. In the wilderness the Lord Jesus faced the same voice, hungry and alone, and answered every suggestion with the word of God (Matthew 4:1–11). He did not win for himself only. Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). That is why Paul’s fear never became despair. The church in Thessalonica faced a defeated enemy, and it had a Saviour who knew that enemy’s voice from the inside.

In vain. In vain is kenos, the empty word of 2:1, where he insisted his coming had not been empty. Here is the honest underside of that confidence. The apostle who writes so certainly about election in chapter 1 also lay awake fearing his work had come to nothing, and neither cancels the other. Strong faith does not mean the absence of anxiety.

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can be lost. Paul feared that their faith might prove false, which would show his labour fruitless. Timothy’s report proved it genuine.

If true believers cannot be lost, why did Paul fear? Because he could not see their hearts, only their outward profession, and he knew that some who make a start fall away because their faith was never real (Matthew 13:20–21; 1 John 2:19). God’s elect will persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and they persevere by means: warnings, teaching, encouragement, prayer. Paul’s fear moved him to supply those means. So we hold both: unshakeable confidence in God’s keeping, and earnest care that no one drifts. The doctrine of perseverance is not a reason to stop watching over one another. And if you fear that the falling away describes you, the fear is itself a hopeful sign: those whose faith was never real seldom lie awake over it. Bring the fear to Christ, who keeps all who come to him (John 6:37).

How do I tell people the cost without frightening them away? Tell them the truth with the reward in view. Jesus never hid the cost of discipleship, and he never mentioned it without the treasure: whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). Say plainly that following Christ may cost friendships, comfort and reputation. Then say why it is worth it: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope, Christ himself. People who are told the truth are not easily shaken when the trouble comes.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy has come back with good news of their faith and love, and it is like new life to Paul. He cannot thank God enough, prays to see them again and supply what their faith still lacks, and asks God to make their love overflow and their hearts blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two persons, one verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb: the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v. 10) was not sincerity but completeness: the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but “for all” (v. 12), the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now that Timothy has come. The letter changes temperature: the news has arrived. Timothy had rejoined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and this letter was written in the first glow of his report.

Good news. Timothy, Paul says, gospelled us (euangelizomai), the only place in his letters where he uses the verb of anything but the gospel of Christ. News that a church was standing firm was, to him, good news of God’s work in the world. Faith and love: their bond with God, and with one another.

Three answers to three fears. Timothy’s report answered each of Paul’s fears. Their faith: they had not been coaxed away. Their love: the community had not turned on itself. And they remembered him kindly: they had not concluded that he abandoned them.

Remember us kindly. Paul had left in the night and not come back, and his enemies had a ready-made accusation. He had been anxious whether they still thought well of him. The slanders had not worked, and the affection ran both ways.

Comforted about you. The apostle is comforted by the young converts. He was in Corinth by now, in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3), and the Lord had to tell him in a vision not to be afraid (Acts 18:9–10).

The traffic runs both ways. In a healthy church the strengtheners are themselves held up by the perseverance of ordinary believers they worry about. If you have ever wondered whether your quiet faithfulness matters to anyone, this verse answers: it was what got Paul through Corinth.

Comfort that flows through Christ. Where does comfort like this come from? Paul answers in another letter written out of deep trouble: as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (2 Corinthians 1:5). The news Timothy carried was good because it was news of Christ at work: faith in him still standing, love for his people still flowing. Paul was comforted through their faith, but the faith was Christ’s gift, and so was the comfort, carried a long way down the road by a young man’s feet. Christ comforts his servants by keeping his people.

Is it all right to care what people think of me? It is right to care about being loved by your brothers and sisters, and to be grieved when relationships are damaged by slander. Paul did. What is wrong is letting their opinion govern your obedience (2:4). Paul would have preached the same gospel whether they thought well of him or not, but he was glad, deeply, that they did. Love wants to be loved back, and that is not vanity.

On a Tuesday. Think of a pastor, parent or mentor who has worried about you, and send them a word this week: how you are doing, and thanks. When you hear good news of someone’s faith, pass it on; it may be the best thing a weary servant hears all month.

For worship. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isaiah 52:7). God sent such feet to a frightened apostle in Corinth: a young man coming down the road with word that a church was still standing. And behind every such messenger stands the news the prophet first announced, that our God reigns and has bared his holy arm to save (Isaiah 52:7–10), the salvation he has now accomplished in his Son. Every report of a believer still standing is a small echo of that great announcement, the God who reigns stooping to cheer one tired man in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we live. Paul does not say he is relieved or encouraged, though he is both. He says he is alive. The months of not knowing had been a kind of death, and Timothy’s news brought him back.

Love makes you a hostage. This is not the unhealthy dependence of a leader whose identity rests on his people’s performance; Paul has insisted he sought no glory from them. It is love, and love always makes your wellbeing hostage to someone else’s. That is not a defect in love; it is what love is.

Standing fast. The word is stēkō, to stand firm, a word that suits a soldier holding his position in the line. Paul uses it repeatedly of churches under pressure (Philippians 1:27; 4:1). It is not a word for advancing or achieving. It means you were still there when the pushing stopped.

In the Lord. And the qualification matters: standing fast in the Lord. Not standing by willpower, or by stubbornness, or by loyalty to Paul. The place they were holding was a person, and their strength was his. He had said of his sheep that no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and a church standing fast in the Lord is a church being held by him. The if is also a gentle encouragement: keep standing.

What does standing firm look like when I feel weak? It looks like still being there. Standing fast is not feeling strong; it is not leaving your post. It means you keep praying when prayer is dry, keep gathering with God’s people when you would rather stay home, keep refusing the sin that keeps coming back, and keep trusting Christ when you do not understand what he is doing. Because you stand in the Lord, your weakness does not decide the outcome. He holds the line with you.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you? It is a real question, not a rhetorical flourish, and Paul does not answer it. He has run out of ways to say thank you. The joy is larger than the vocabulary available for it. And the thanks goes to God, since he is the one who kept them.

Before our God. The joy is felt before our God: not a private gladness but something brought into God’s presence and held up there, because he is the one who did it.

Most earnestly night and day. The word (hyperekperissou) is a piled-up compound: beyond, beyond measure. And night and day is the phrase he used in 2:9 of working at his trade. Whatever else Paul was doing at night, he was not sleeping much.

Face to face. The longing of 2:17 has not cooled. Letters are not enough.

And supply what is lacking in your faith? This phrase needs care, because it can sound like a rebuke, and it is not one. Paul has just spent eight verses celebrating their faith. The word is katartizō, to put a thing into working order: it is used of the disciples mending their nets (Matthew 4:21), of a doctor setting a bone, and of God equipping his people for every good work (Hebrews 13:21). What is lacking is not sincerity but completeness: the teaching he never had time to give in a stay of a few weeks. Chapters 4 and 5 begin to supply it, on holiness, love, and the return of Christ.

Already full in Christ. What could be lacking in their faith? Not Christ. Paul tells another young church that in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him (Colossians 2:9–10). Nothing missing in the Thessalonians would be supplied by adding something alongside Christ: a technique, a secret experience, a further teacher. It would be supplied by knowing more of the Christ they already had, and that is what the rest of the letter does, teaching them the holiness he wills, the love he teaches and the return he has promised. Growth in faith is always growth into Christ, never away from him to something more.

How do I know what is lacking in my faith? There is a deficiency that is a fault, and there is a deficiency that is simply an unfinished education: gaps where nobody ever taught you. Paul’s response to the second is not reproach. It is to want to come and fill them in. So ask honestly: where do I not know what the Bible teaches? Where do I believe but not obey? Where does fear still rule? Then seek the remedy God provides: sit under faithful preaching, read whole books of Scripture, ask a mature believer to help you, and pray for growth. Gaps are expected; staying content with them is not.

Is my faith real if it has gaps? Yes. Every believer’s faith is incomplete in this life. The Thessalonians had a famous faith (1:8) that still lacked things. Real faith is not perfect faith; it is faith that rests on Christ and wants to grow. The fact that you notice gaps and want them filled is itself a sign of life.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father and the Lord Jesus. Two subjects, the Father and the Lord Jesus, and in the Greek the verb is singular. Paul names two persons and speaks of their acting as one, without explanation or apology; it is simply how he prays. A prayer addressed to the Father and the Son together assumes that the Son is God, and it shows how early and how instinctively the highest view of Christ was in place.

In the flow. Verses 11 to 13 are a prayer that closes the first half of the letter and opens the second. Chapters 1 to 3 have looked back on Paul’s visit, his absence and Timothy’s report. Now he asks for three things: a clear road back to them (v. 11), love that overflows (v. 12), and hearts made holy for Christ’s coming (v. 13). Chapters 4 and 5 then take up those very themes: holiness (4:1–8), love (4:9–12) and the coming of the Lord (4:13–5:11). Paul prays first for what he is about to teach.

Direct our way to you. The verb (kateuthynō) means to make straight, to clear a road, the opposite of Satan cutting into it (2:18). The enemy genuinely obstructs, and the Sovereign genuinely governs, and only one of them is being prayed to.

What Paul does with frustration. He does not rebuke the devil, and he does not strategise. He asks God to clear the road, and gets on with the work he can do from where he is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are one person. They are distinct persons who act as one God.

Is it right to pray to Jesus, or only to the Father? Both are right. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). But Scripture also shows believers praying to Jesus directly: Stephen called on him as he died (Acts 7:59), Paul pleaded with the Lord about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8), and here he prays to the Father and the Son together. Because the Son is God, he may be addressed in prayer and worshipped. You will not offend the Father by speaking to his Son.

What should I make of it when God does not answer my prayer the way I asked? Keep praying, and keep watching for what he does instead. Paul did not get his visit for years, but God answered the deeper request: the church was strengthened and Paul’s love reached them, through a letter. God always hears his children, and he gives what we would ask for if we knew what he knows. A no or a not yet from a wise Father is still an answer, and often a better one.

For worship. The Father and the Son act as one, and they rule every road on earth. No enemy can close what they open, and no door they shut is shut by accident. The same Lord Jesus who is addressed in this prayer is the way to the Father, and he has made the road to God straight for us by his blood. Every road his people travel, blocked or open, runs at last to his Father’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Increase and abound in love. The second petition asks for love, and the verbs are extravagant. The first (pleonazō) means to multiply, to grow more; the second (perisseuō) to overflow, like a river over its banks. Paul is not asking that they manage to be reasonably loving. He is asking for a flood.

For one another and for all. The second phrase is the sharp one. A community under hostility naturally turns inward, and its warmth becomes reserved for insiders: understandable, and the beginning of a sect. Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow with love toward the very population making its life difficult, including its persecutors (Matthew 5:44).

As we do for you. Paul offers his own affection as the measure, having spent two chapters demonstrating what it looked like in practice.

Who produces it. May the Lord make you increase: Paul asks God to do it in them rather than telling them to try harder. The commands come in chapter 4, but the order is the order everywhere in his letters: ask God for what you then go and work at.

Blameless in holiness. Establish is the buttressing word of verse 2 (stērizō): what Timothy was sent to do, Paul now asks God to do. Love leads to holiness, and blameless means without just accusation. Holiness means being set apart for God and made like him in character. That is no small request, because the God before whom they will stand is the one the seraphim call holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3), and before whom even Isaiah cried that he was undone. Holiness is also where the letter turns next (4:3).

Before our God and Father. In his presence, at the judgement. The goal of the Christian life is to stand before the Father with nothing that can be justly charged against us.

With all his saints. Christ’s return, the parousia again. His saints, his holy ones, may be the angels who accompany him (Matthew 25:31), on the pattern of Zechariah 14:5, where the LORD comes and all the holy ones with him; or believers who have died, whom God will bring with him (4:14); or both. Paul has borrowed a prophet’s picture of the LORD arriving in judgement and applied it, without comment, to Jesus.

Where Christians differ: coming for his saints, or with them? Some dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras and expect separate futures for Israel and the church) distinguish Christ coming for his saints (a secret rapture) from coming with his saints (seven years later). They hold it out of a careful reading of prophecy and a real longing for Christ’s appearing, and this commentary honours them as brothers. Verdict: Paul describes one coming, at which Christ brings the souls of departed believers with him, raises their bodies, gathers the living, and judges the world (4:14–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). He comes both for and with his saints in a single, visible, glorious return. There is no secret rapture. Paul’s second letter adds that this one coming will be preceded by the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3): it is near and certain, but it will not come unheralded.

How can anyone be blameless before God? In two ways, both by grace. First, believers are already counted righteous in Christ: his perfect obedience and his death are credited to them, so that no charge can stand (Romans 8:33–34). Second, God is making them holy in fact, a work he begins at conversion and completes at Christ’s coming, when we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). Theologians call the first justification, God declaring the guilty righteous for Christ’s sake, and the second sanctification, God making them holy over a lifetime. Paul prays for the second on the basis of the first. You will stand blameless on that day not because you finally got it right, but because Christ did, and because the God who began the work will finish it (5:23–24).

How do I love people who make my life difficult? Start by asking God for it, as Paul does; it is his gift before it is your effort. Then do concrete good: pray for them specifically, speak well of them where you honestly can, refuse revenge, and look for a practical kindness. Love is not pretending the harm did not happen, and it does not require you to stay in danger or to trust someone who has not changed. But it does wish them good, and it leaves judgement to God.
