4.title: Holy Living and the Blessed Hope
4.overview: Paul now fills in what he could not teach in a few weeks. First, holiness, above all sexual purity, in a city where sex outside marriage was socially normal for men. Second, love and work: they are already “taught by God” to love one another, and should live quietly and work with their hands. Third, the question that had shaken them: what happens to believers who die before Jesus returns? They are not lost. Because Jesus died and rose, the dead in Christ will rise first, the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord, and so we will always be with the Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–8 – The Will of God Is Your Sanctification
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks them to keep growing in the life that pleases God. God’s will is their holiness: keeping clear of sexual immorality, governing their own bodies honourably, and never wronging a fellow believer. To dismiss this teaching is to dismiss God, who gives them his Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The body, and who lives in it

Paul grounds Christian sexual ethics not in his own authority or in respectability but in the Holy Spirit, whom God goes on giving to the believer (v. 8). The claim on the Christian’s body is not that God is restrictive but that God has moved in (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property; Paul brought a different account of what a person is, and applied one standard to men and women alike.

Now: Verse 6 names the victim: sexual sin is always something done to a person, and the Lord is an avenger for those who never had redress.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, then, brothers, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 4 begins to supply what was lacking in their faith (3:10). First, holiness: God’s will is their sanctification, especially sexual purity; each must control his body in holiness and honour, not in lust like pagans who do not know God, and must not wrong a brother, for God calls to holiness and gives his Holy Spirit (vv. 1–8). Second, love and work: they love one another and should do so more, living quietly and working with their hands so as to earn the respect of outsiders (vv. 9–12). Third, hope: some of their number had died, and they feared these would miss Christ’s return. Christians grieve, but not without hope, because Jesus died and rose. When the Lord descends with a shout, the dead in Christ will rise first, the living will be caught up with them to meet him, and so they will always be with the Lord (vv. 13–18). The chapter is Paul’s prayer for love and holiness at Christ’s coming (3:12–13) turned into instruction.

Finally, then, brothers. Finally (loipon) does not mean Paul is winding up; it means for the rest, and marks the turn from report to request. What follows is his prayer that God would establish their hearts blameless in holiness (3:13), spelled out as instructions.

Ask and urge. One verb is the ordinary word for a request; the other is parakaleō, to come alongside and appeal. Neither is a bare command, from a man who had every right to issue one (2:6). And he appeals in the Lord Jesus, with the Lord’s own authority behind it.

To please God. Not a rulebook but a relationship: the aim of Christian conduct is that a Person is pleased. You can satisfy a rule without ever thinking of the one who gave it; you cannot please a person that way. Christian ethics is a life that delights God.

More and more. Before he corrects anything he confirms that they are on the road. More and more comes twice in this chapter (vv. 1, 10), and it is the letter’s characteristic note.

Instructions through the Lord Jesus. The word parangelia means instructions or orders, the kind a superior passes down, and it could be used of military commands. These were never Paul’s orders. They came through him from the Lord Jesus, and he was as much under them as they were.

All that I have commanded you. Paul’s instructions to new converts were the Lord’s own commission being carried out. The risen Christ, with all authority in heaven and on earth, sent his apostles to make disciples, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you (Matthew 28:18–20). So Paul was handing on Christ’s orders in Christ’s name. And the Lord who gives them said, if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15). His commands come from the one who loved us first, which is why they are not burdensome (1 John 5:3).

If I fail, is God displeased with me as his child? In Christ you are accepted completely and permanently; your standing as God’s child rests on Christ’s obedience, not yours, and your failures do not undo your adoption (Romans 8:1, 15). But a loving Father can be grieved by what his children do, and glad when they obey, and Scripture speaks of both (Ephesians 4:30; Colossians 1:10). So you live from acceptance, not for it, and you can actually bring God pleasure, which is one of the most astonishing things the Bible says about ordinary believers.

Why does Paul say more and more if they are already doing well? Because the Christian life is growth, not maintenance. Doing well is never a reason to stop; it is the ground for going further. Paul is teaching a way of encouragement worth copying: name what is good honestly, then call for growth from there. Nobody arrives in this life. The best believers you know are the ones still learning to please God more.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your sanctification. People often say they wish they knew the will of God for their lives. Paul states it here in a single sentence, and it is not about a job or a marriage or a city. It is your sanctification (hagiasmos), being made holy. Whatever else God may or may not disclose about your circumstances, this much is published: he intends to make you holy.

By that will. God’s will for our holiness was first a will his Son came to do. Hebrews puts Psalm 40 in Christ’s mouth, I have come to do your will, O God, and adds that by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:7–10). So sanctification has two sides. Believers have already been set apart as God’s holy people by Christ’s body given on the cross; now, in their own bodies, they are being made holy in fact. In practice: you are not trying to become God’s by keeping pure. You are already his, bought by a body offered for you, and purity is learning to live as what you are.

Abstain from sexual immorality. The first application is the body. Abstain (apechomai) means keep away from, keep your distance. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word covering every sexual act outside marriage between a man and a woman, the union Jesus grounds in the creation of male and female (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).

The world it landed in. Greco-Roman sexual ethics were governed by status and property, not by any notion that the body was sacred. A married man’s use of slaves, prostitutes and concubines was socially unremarkable; what was policed was another citizen’s wife, because that was theft. A speech from fourth-century BC Athens, preserved under Demosthenes’ name, could set out the arrangement without embarrassment, and not much had changed by Paul’s day: courtesans for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives for legitimate children. Into that Paul says the body is not a piece of property governed by appetite, and that the same standard applies to men and women alike. It was not a tightening of existing morality. It was a different account of what a person is.

Control his own body. Verse 4 contains a genuine translation question, as the ESV footnote notes. The word is skeuos, vessel or instrument, used of the body (2 Corinthians 4:7) and of a wife (1 Peter 3:7). It may mean the body, and so self-control (as the ESV takes it); or it may mean a wife, and so know how to take a wife for himself in holiness and honour rather than in lust. Both readings are defensible and old.

Which reading is more likely? The ESV’s body is the more likely: the context is self-control in sexual matters, and the command is given to each one of you, single and married. Either way the point is the same: sexual life is to be lived in holiness and honour, which rules out treating a person as an instrument for one’s own appetite, and that is precisely what both readings forbid.

Like the Gentiles who do not know God. Paul draws a straight line from ignorance of God to disordered desire (pathos epithymias, the passion of craving). He is not saying pagans were uniquely wicked; the ancient world had moralists who taught restraint. He is saying that when God is not known, there is no reason the body should be treated as anything but a means of pleasure, and that the reason a Christian treats it otherwise is not superior willpower but knowledge of God. Those who know God have both a reason and a power to be pure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sex itself is unholy. Within marriage it is God’s good gift (1 Corinthians 7:3–5; Hebrews 13:4). It means sexual desire must be governed by holiness.

Does sexual immorality include things like pornography or living together before marriage? Yes. Porneia covers every sexual act outside the marriage of one man and one woman, and Jesus took the standard into the heart: looking at someone with lustful intent is adultery there (Matthew 5:28). Pornography trains the heart in exactly the lust Paul describes and uses real people as instruments. Living together as though married, without marriage, takes the gift without the covenant. The call is not to shame but to holiness: get out of the situation, bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and take the practical steps that make purity possible.

I have already sinned sexually. Can I be made clean? Yes, completely. Paul lists the sexually immoral among those who will not inherit the kingdom, and then says: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Christ’s blood cleanses every sin confessed to him (1 John 1:9). You may live with consequences, and you may need help to break patterns, but you are not second-class. In Christ you are clean, and holiness from here on is possible.

What about desires I did not choose? Being tempted is not the same as sinning. The Lord Jesus himself felt the full pressure of temptation and never once gave way (Hebrews 4:15). Many Christians carry desires they did not choose and would not choose, whether for sex outside marriage, for the same sex, or simply strong desire with no spouse. The call to each is the same: do not feed the desire, do not act on it, bring it honestly to God, and find support in the church. Singleness lived in purity is not a lesser life; it is a holy one, and the Lord Jesus lived it.

On a Tuesday. Identify the place where your purity is most tested: a device, a time of night, a relationship, a habit of thought. Make one concrete change there today: move the phone, install accountability, end the conversation, tell a trusted believer. The Spirit who lives in you is the power for purity, and he seldom gives it as heroic resistance in the moment; usually it comes through wise decisions made beforehand.
verseByVerse.note: To “control his own body” may instead mean “take a wife for himself”; the phrase can be read either way.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you beforehand and solemnly warned you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wrong his brother. This is the verse that gives the passage its teeth, because it names the victim. Up to now the argument has been about holiness and the will of God. Now Paul says that sexual sin is also, always, something done to a person. Transgress (hyperbainō) means to overstep a boundary. Wrong (pleonekteō) is from the root meaning to have more: to overreach, to take advantage, to defraud, a word at home in business dealings. Paul uses it of sexual sin because that is what it is: taking from someone something that was not yours, to get more for yourself.

Sexual sin is never private. That cuts through a great deal of modern discussion, in which sexual behaviour between consenting adults is treated as a private matter affecting nobody. Paul’s category is different. There is a brother or sister on the other side of it: the person used, the spouse betrayed, the family fractured, the future spouse defrauded. Adultery defrauds a husband or wife; sex before marriage defrauds a future spouse and the other person. Sin here is not merely impurity; it is theft from a person Christ died for.

An avenger. The word is ekdikos: the one who brings justice for the wronged (compare Hebrews 13:4; Ephesians 5:5–6). Sexual sin very often goes unpunished in this life and its victims frequently get no hearing at all; the powerful have generally been able to use people and keep their reputation. Paul says there is a court that does not work that way. Even when no human court acts, God sees. To the person who has been wronged and never had redress, this verse is not a threat but a promise.

The Lord who avenges. The Lord here is most likely the Lord Jesus, whom Paul’s next letter describes revealed from heaven in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8), the very phrase just used of the pagans (4:5). The one who will right every sexual wrong took children in his arms and blessed them, and warned that it would be better to be drowned with a millstone round the neck than to cause one of these little ones to stumble (Mark 10:16; Matthew 18:6). His tenderness toward the vulnerable and his anger at those who use them are the same love.

Told you beforehand. He had said all this while he was with them. Sexual ethics was part of the basic instruction given to new converts, not a new severity sprung on people recruited on easier terms.

A word to those on the wrong side of it. Paul’s letters are always written to actual sinners. The God who is an avenger for the wronged is the same God who, three verses earlier, is named as the one who makes people holy. The passage exists because such people can be changed. It is a warning precisely because there is a way out: confess, turn, make what restitution can be made, and run to Christ.

I was the one wronged. What does this verse say to me? It says God is on your side. What was done to you was a real wrong, an overstepping and a theft, not a misunderstanding, and God takes it personally. If you were abused, it was never your fault, and the church must never hide or tolerate it: report it to the authorities, seek safety, and find people who will care for you. God’s promise to avenge means you do not have to carry the burden of making it right yourself. He will judge justly, and in Christ he can also heal what was broken.

For worship. The Lord is an avenger, and that is good news for every victim the world forgot. No wrong escapes him. And the same Lord bore the punishment for every sinner who flees to him, so that the avenger of the wronged is also the Saviour of the wrongdoer who repents. Justice and mercy meet in him. He is the God who sees, as a wronged slave-girl once found in the desert (Genesis 16:13), and nothing done in the dark is hidden from him.

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Called in holiness. The calling determines the character. Paul does not argue from consequences or from health or from social order; he argues from what these people were summoned into (1 Peter 1:15–16). Impurity (akatharsia, uncleanness) is the opposite of what God called us to. Holiness is not an advanced option for keen Christians. It is the content of the invitation.

Not man but God. The escalation is deliberate. The verb (atheteō) means to set aside as having no authority. Paul does not say, I am an apostle, so obey me; he has refused that move. He says the instruction was never his (v. 2, through the Lord Jesus), so setting it aside is not a disagreement with Paul at all. There is nobody in between to argue with.

Who gives his Holy Spirit. And then the ground, which is the heart of the paragraph. Two details. The tense is present and continuous: not who once gave, but who goes on giving. (Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read who has given; the present is better supported, and most modern Bibles follow it.) And the preposition is into you. The Holy Spirit dwells in believers (1 Corinthians 6:19).

An argument that ends with a Person. So the argument for sexual holiness ends not with a threat but with a Person. The Spirit is not a force issued at conversion and filed away; he is continually given, and lives in the very body under discussion. That is why this is not moralism. Paul does not argue from purity codes or social respectability; he asks them to consider who is inside them. He makes the same argument to Corinth: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, you are not your own, you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The Christian’s body is not his own property, not because God is restrictive but because God has moved in. Sexual sin grieves him; and he gives the power to be holy.

Poured out by the exalted Son. The Spirit God gives is the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), poured out by the risen Christ: exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, Jesus poured out what the crowd at Pentecost saw and heard (Acts 2:33). So the Spirit inside a believer’s body is the fruit of Christ’s cross and ascension, and his work has a shape: we are being transformed into the same image, from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The holiness Paul asks for is Christ’s likeness, formed by Christ’s Spirit.

Was this not just Paul’s culture? Our culture has moved on. The culture of Paul’s day was far more permissive than his teaching, not less, so this was never simply his culture talking; it was the gospel confronting it. And Paul says plainly that this instruction comes from the Lord Jesus and that rejecting it is rejecting God. Cultures change, but the God who made our bodies and the Spirit who lives in them do not. What feels old-fashioned in one century is often what the next century discovers it needed.

If the Spirit lives in me, why do I still struggle with lust? Because the Spirit’s presence starts a war; it does not end one at once. The flesh desires against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17), and every believer fights until glory. The struggle itself is a sign of his presence: unbelievers are rarely troubled by lust in this way. Keep fighting by the means he gives: Scripture, prayer, confession, accountability, fleeing temptation, and filling your life with better things. He who gives his Spirit continually will not abandon the fight in you.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:9–12 – Brotherly Love and the Quiet Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has taught them to love one another, and they should do so more and more. They should also aim to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they depend on no one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The new covenant, arrived

In calling them “taught by God”, Paul reaches for Jeremiah’s new covenant promise that God would write his law on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33–34). His evidence that it has arrived among these former pagans is not their doctrine but their love, which is the more striking because he was driven out before he could teach them much.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some may have stopped working because they expected the Lord’s return at any moment; by the second letter the problem had grown (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12).

Now: Expecting the Lord’s return should make a Christian more reliable, not less, and idleness that lives off others is a failure of love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another, for that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning brotherly love. Paul turns to philadelphia, love for fellow believers as family, perhaps a subject they had asked about. You have no need for anyone to write to you, he says, and then writes anyway: a gracious way of raising a subject they already know.

Taught by God. The reason is a word found in no earlier Greek writing that survives. They have been theodidaktoi, God-taught. Paul may well have coined it, and he is almost certainly reaching for Jeremiah’s new covenant promise: I will put my law within them, I will write it on their hearts, and they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:33–34; John 6:45; 1 John 2:27).

The new covenant has landed. That is a considerable claim about a congregation of former pagans a few months old. The promised new covenant had visibly arrived among them, not because they had excellent teaching, since Paul had only weeks with them, but because God had written it inside them.

The new covenant in his blood. The covenant Jeremiah promised was not established by a lecture. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took the cup and said, this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). God-taught love was learned at that table and that cross, and Jesus gave the lesson in a sentence: a new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another (John 13:34). The pattern of the love is his, and so is its power.

Throughout Macedonia. The love had travelled beyond their own congregation, perhaps through hospitality to travellers and gifts for the needy. A young, poor, persecuted church reaching outside its walls is not the natural behaviour of a frightened minority; it is the answer to Paul’s prayer that they would abound in love for one another and for all (3:12). Having praised them warmly, Paul asks for more, and the request grows out of the praise.

How can I love a fellow believer I find difficult? Remember that God taught you to love, not to like; affection may follow, but love begins with will and action. Bring them to God in prayer; it is hard to keep resenting someone you pray for. Look for Christ in them, since he lives in them as he does in you. Do them good in small, concrete ways. Overlook what can be overlooked, and speak honestly and gently about what cannot (Matthew 18:15). And remember that someone in your church is probably finding you difficult too.

What does loving believers in other churches look like? It looks like what the Thessalonians did for all the brothers in Macedonia: hospitality, prayer, practical help. Pray for other congregations in your town by name, especially those faithful to the gospel. Welcome visiting believers. Give to churches in need, here and abroad. Speak well of other gospel churches rather than competing with them. Brotherly love does not stop at your own front door.

For worship. Many in that church had lost their families when they turned from the household gods, and God gave them brothers and sisters across a whole province. The Son of God is not ashamed to call such people his brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The Firstborn has sat down with former idol-worshippers, made them children of his own Father, and set them at one table. A family bought with blood and written on the heart by the Spirit is the one family no persecution can break up, and its love is the Father’s own love for his Son, overflowing.

verseByVerse.quote: and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aspire to live quietly. The first of three instructions is almost a joke in Greek. Philotimeomai means to be ambitious, to make it your point of honour, the word for a man competing for public distinction; Paul joins it to hēsychazō, to be quiet. Make it your ambition to be unremarkable, not a busybody or an agitator.

Mind your own affairs. The natural companion: attend to your own business rather than everyone else’s (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

Work with your hands. The practical outworking, and it was an affront to Greek sensibility. Manual labour was what slaves and the poor did; a man with philosophical pretensions did not sit at a bench. Paul, who had done exactly that among them night and day (2:9), tells them to do it too.

Why this needed saying. Perhaps partly because of the hope Paul turns to next, though he does not say so, and the explanation should be held lightly. If the Lord is returning imminently, some may have concluded, why keep working, plan or save? Some may also have expected wealthier believers to support them. The problem grew worse: in the second letter Paul addresses those who are not busy at work but busybodies, and says that if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12).

Hope makes you more reliable. So this is the first appearance of a principle the letter will keep insisting on: expecting the Lord’s return should make you more reliable, not less. The person who stops working because Jesus is coming has misunderstood what he is coming for. And idleness here is treated as a failure of love: the idle man’s food comes from somewhere, and the somewhere is his brothers.

Found at work when he comes. The Lord Jesus had already drawn the connection. Of the faithful servant left in charge of his master’s household he said, blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes (Luke 12:43). Whether a servant thinks the master delayed or coming tomorrow, if he stops working he has misread his master. Christ’s people wait by doing the ordinary work in front of them, and the best way to be ready for him is to be found at the bench, the desk or the sink, doing it for him.

Properly before outsiders. Properly (euschēmonōs) means decently, respectably: the watching city again (1:8). An honest, working, unhysterical church is an argument for the gospel; a community of excitable freeloaders is an argument for the other side. And be dependent on no one is not a rejection of Christian generosity, which Paul commends everywhere, but the refusal to become a weight on people when you need not be.

Does live quietly mean Christians should stay out of public life? No. Paul is not forbidding Christians from holding office, voting, speaking for justice or serving their city; elsewhere he used his citizenship and appealed to Caesar. He is forbidding restlessness, meddling and agitation: the busybody who manages everyone else’s business and neglects his own. A Christian may serve in public life, but with a quiet spirit, faithful in ordinary duties, not stirring up trouble or seeking to be noticed.

What if I cannot work, or cannot find work? Then this verse is not a rebuke to you. Paul’s target is those who can work and will not. The sick, the elderly, the disabled, those caring for others, and those looking for work and not finding it are to be cared for by the church gladly (1 Timothy 5:3–16; Galatians 6:10). Do what you can, receive help without shame, and remember that your worth to God was never measured by your wages. Faithful prayer and quiet kindness are work in his eyes.

On a Tuesday. There is a quiet dignity here that our own age needs. The New Testament’s ambition for most Christians is not a platform or a public voice. It is a life of ordinary competence: your own work done well, your own business minded, your bills paid, and nobody made poorer by having you around. Do today’s work as service to the Lord, and leave one piece of other people’s business alone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some believers had died, and the church feared they would miss the Lord’s return. Paul writes so that they will not grieve like people with no hope: the dead in Christ will rise first, the living will be gathered with them to meet the Lord, and they will always be with him. They are to comfort one another with this.
verseByVerse.theology:
The meeting on the road

“To meet the Lord” (v. 17) is the language of a city’s delegation going out along the road to greet an arriving king and escort him in (Acts 28:15). The passage describes one loud, public, personal arrival, and it gives no timetable.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Against the bleak tomb inscriptions of that world, a Christian funeral in Thessalonica must have looked extraordinary: the same tears, and something else altogether.

Now: Paul does not forbid grief, only grief without hope (v. 13); and the passage is for comforting one another at gravesides (v. 18), not for building charts.

verseByVerse.quote: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not uninformed. Here is the pastoral emergency behind the letter, probably raised by Timothy’s report. Some in the church had died, and the congregation was in distress. Paul had taught them to wait for the Son from heaven (1:10), but in a stay of a few weeks he had not covered what happens to a believer who dies before the Lord arrives. Would they miss it? Had they lost their place? Paul’s answer to grief is information. He does not tell them to feel differently or to pray harder; he tells them a fact they did not know, because not knowing it was the cause of their distress. Sometimes what the grieving need is not more comfort but the truth.

Those who are asleep. The verb is koimaomai, the New Testament’s usual word for the death of a believer (John 11:11; Acts 7:60; 1 Corinthians 15:18); our word cemetery comes from the same root, and it means a sleeping place. What the metaphor carries is that death is temporary and that there will be a waking. You do not put a person to bed forever. Some of the Thessalonian believers had died since Paul left, perhaps through persecution, perhaps of ordinary illness.

Sleep is Jesus’ word. The word is not a soft euphemism invented to spare feelings; it is the Lord’s own. He told his disciples, our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him (John 11:11). They thought he meant rest. He meant death, and that death in his presence is something he can wake people from. Christians call their dead asleep because Jesus did, and because he proved it at a tomb. Death is only sleep when the one who speaks over it is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

Not as others do. Now the sentence that matters most, and it must be read exactly. Paul does not forbid grief (lypeō). The qualifier is the whole point. Christians grieve; they do not grieve like people with nothing ahead.

Grief is not a failure of faith. Bereaved believers have been made to feel that tears are a failure of faith, and that is a cruelty this verse does not support. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to open (John 11:35). Grief is love with nowhere to put itself, and it is right. What Christian hope changes is not whether you weep but what you know while you are weeping.

Who have no hope. This was simply accurate. The tomb inscriptions of that world are bleak reading: one Latin formula, common enough to be abbreviated on gravestones, ran, I was not, I was, I am not, I care not. A common consolation was that nobody has ever come back, so grieve and be done. Against that, Christian funerals in Thessalonica must have looked extraordinary: the same tears, and something else entirely.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Some sincere Christians take asleep to mean the souls of the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Verdict: Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The souls of believers are immediately with Christ, consciously and joyfully (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43). God will bring them with Jesus (v. 14): they are with him now. Their bodies sleep until the resurrection, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1).

How long is it right to grieve? There is no set time. Grief for someone you love may soften but rarely disappears completely, and it often returns at anniversaries, songs and empty chairs. Christian hope does not put a deadline on tears; it puts a floor under them. If grief so overwhelms you for a long time that you cannot function, eat, sleep or pray, that is not a lack of faith, but it is a sign to seek help from your pastor, your doctor or a trusted counsellor. Let the church carry you.

What about loved ones who died without faith in Christ? This is the hardest grief, and Paul’s comfort here is for those who die in Christ. Scripture does not offer hope of salvation apart from Christ, and we must not invent one. But we also do not know what passed between a person and God in their last days or hours; the thief on the cross was saved at the very end. So we neither pronounce on them nor pretend. We leave them to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right, and we grieve honestly. And we hold fast to Christ ourselves, and speak of him to the living while there is time.

For worship. God has turned death into sleep for his people. The grave is not a pit but a bed, and the morning is coming, because the one who will wake them went down into the darkest night himself and came back at dawn. The gravestones of that world said, I care not. Heaven’s answer is a Saviour who knows each of his sleeping friends by name and will not leave one of them in the dust. Our grief is real, and his resurrection is more real still.
verseByVerse.note: “Asleep” was a common Christian way of speaking of believers who had died.

verseByVerse.quote: For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus died and rose again. Paul’s argument is one sentence long and it rests entirely on a historical event. This is the foundation of hope: not a theory about the soul, but the empty tomb.

Union, not analogy. It is not that Jesus’ resurrection makes resurrection seem plausible in general; it is that these people are in him, and what happened to the head happens to the body. Paul spells it out to Corinth: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). The first sheaf of a harvest is not a hopeful sign that a harvest might follow. It is the beginning of the harvest itself.

Died, and fallen asleep. Of Jesus Paul says died; of believers he says fallen asleep. He will not soften Golgotha. Jesus died in the full and terrible sense, bearing the curse of death itself, and precisely because he took death whole it has become sleep for everybody else.

God will bring with him. Two things follow, answering their fear directly. The dead are not left behind: when Jesus comes, they come with him. And they are not lost in the meantime: their souls are already with Christ, which is why they can accompany him, to be reunited with their raised bodies.

Through Jesus. The phrase can attach either to the sleeping or to the bringing: those who have fallen asleep through Jesus, as believers, or God will bring them through Jesus, through his saving work. Either way, everything about a Christian’s death and future runs through the same person.

Is this not just wishful thinking, a story people tell to cope with death? Wishful thinking produces vague hopes: that the dead live on in our memories, or in the stars. Paul’s hope rests on a public claim about a particular tomb outside Jerusalem, made within twenty years of the event, when hundreds of witnesses were still alive to be questioned (1 Corinthians 15:6). And the first Christians were Jews, most of whom expected the righteous to rise together at the end of history, not one man in the middle of it. People do not easily invent a hope that cuts across everything they expected. The first witnesses said they believed it because they had seen him, and many of them suffered for saying so. If he did not rise, Paul says, Christians are to be pitied (1 Corinthians 15:17–19); if he did, death is not the end of anyone who belongs to him.

Does it matter what happens to the body: burial, cremation, lost at sea? God can raise any body, however it was lost; the martyrs burned and the sailors drowned are not beyond his reach (Revelation 20:13). Many Christians prefer burial because it pictures the body sown in hope, as the Lord’s body was laid in a tomb, and it honours the body as something God will raise. Others choose cremation for good reasons, and it does not affect anyone’s resurrection. Whatever is done, treat the body with honour, because it belonged to someone God loves and will one day stand again.

Why does the resurrection of the body matter, if the soul is already with Christ? Because God made us body and soul, and salvation is the rescue of the whole person. Being with Christ now is far better (Philippians 1:23), but it is not the end. Death tears apart what God joined, and the resurrection puts it back together, glorified. Christian hope is not escape from the body but the redemption of the body (Romans 8:23), in a renewed creation.

verseByVerse.quote: For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word from the Lord. What follows is not Paul’s inference but revelation: a saying of Jesus not recorded in the Gospels, a direct revelation to Paul, or a summary of Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 24:30–31). Paul is careful about this distinction elsewhere (1 Corinthians 7:10, 12), so the flag can be trusted. Whichever it is, it comes with the Lord’s authority.

Will not precede. The revealed point is deliberately modest: not a timetable, but one fact. Precede (phthanō) means to get ahead of: the living will not get there first. That answers the whole anxiety, the fear that the dead had been left at the back of the queue. Paul says there is no queue.

Did Paul expect to be alive when Christ returned? He writes we who are alive because he identifies himself with whoever will be living then; he did not know when it would be, as he says in the next chapter (5:1–2). Later he speaks of his own death as likely (2 Timothy 4:6). He was not mistaken; he was ready. Some readers think Paul hoped at this stage to live to see it; even if he did, he never taught a date, and nothing he affirmed has failed. Every generation lives ready.

The Lord himself. Then the arrival itself, in three sounds. First, the Lord himself: not an angel sent to fetch them, but this same Jesus who was taken up, coming in person from heaven where he now reigns (1:10; Acts 1:11).

With a cry of command. The word is keleusma, the shout of an officer to troops, or of the man who sets the stroke for rowers: a word of authority, not noise. Perhaps it is the voice that raises the dead, for all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28–29).

With the voice of an archangel. A chief angel, perhaps Michael (Jude 9). The angels who announced his birth and his resurrection will herald his return.

Is Jesus the archangel? Jehovah’s Witnesses teach this, identifying him with Michael. No. The Lord descends with the voice of an archangel, as he descends with the trumpet; the archangel accompanies him. Hebrews says God never called any angel his Son (Hebrews 1:5), and that all God’s angels worship him (Hebrews 1:6).

The trumpet of God. The last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52; Matthew 24:31). In Israel’s Scriptures the trumpet summoned the assembly and announced God’s presence on the mountain (Exodus 19:16). Everything about this is public and loud. Whatever else the passage describes, it does not describe anything secret.

The dead in Christ will rise first. There is the answer, stated flatly: before the living are caught up. In Christ is doing the work. They died in union with him, and that union was never broken; death interrupted only what could be seen of it. What does union with Christ mean? By faith and the Spirit believers are so joined to him that what is his becomes theirs: his death for sin, his new life, and one day his resurrection (Romans 6:5). Their bodies are raised.

Only believers here. Paul says the dead in Christ. He is not giving a general account of the resurrection of all the dead, but answering one grieving congregation about their own, and he stays on the point that was keeping them awake. All will be raised in the end (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15).

What body will the dead in Christ rise with? It will be your body, recognisably you, but transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, and fitted for the life of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The risen Jesus is the pattern: he could be touched, he ate, he bore the marks of his wounds, and yet he was no longer subject to death. Our lowly bodies will be made like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). No more illness, ageing or disability, and no more sin in our members. And those still alive when he comes will be changed in a moment, so that the risen and the living meet him in the same glory (1 Corinthians 15:51–52).

verseByVerse.quote: Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caught up together with them. After the dead are raised. The verb is harpazō: seized, snatched, carried off by force, used of the Spirit carrying Philip away (Acts 8:39). In Latin it became rapiemur, from rapio, which is where the English word rapture comes from. So the word is biblical; the question is what the scene describes. Together with them: living and raised believers reunited, the separation of death undone in an instant. In the clouds: often the sign of God’s presence, at Sinai, at the ascension, and in Daniel’s vision of the Son of Man (Exodus 19:9; Acts 1:9; Daniel 7:13).

To meet the Lord in the air. The decisive term is the next one. To meet the Lord is eis apantēsin, a near-technical phrase. When a king or governor approached a city, the citizens went out along the road in a formal delegation to greet him, and then turned round and escorted him in. The party does not go out and stay out; the point is the entrance. The word is used of the virgins going out to meet the bridegroom (Matthew 25:6), and of the Roman Christians who walked down the Appian Way to meet Paul and bring him into the city (Acts 28:15).

The King comes home. Paul has been building this picture since 2:19, where he called it the parousia, the civic vocabulary of a royal visit. The King arrives; his people, the dead first and then the living, go out to meet him on the way; and the procession comes home. Read like this, the passage is not about the church being removed from the earth. It is about the King coming to it, and his people going out to welcome him and accompany him in triumph. Paul himself does not describe what follows the meeting, so the picture is a pointer rather than a proof; but it fits the rest of Scripture, where the King comes to stay.

What the text supplies, and what it does not. It supplies one loud, public, personal arrival, at which the Christian dead are raised before anyone is caught up. It gives no timetable at all: Paul goes out of his way in the next chapter to say that times and seasons are not the point (5:1–2).

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, with separate futures for Israel and the church) teach a secret, pre-tribulation rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers to heaven, leaving the world to a seven-year tribulation, before returning visibly with them. Those who hold it are often among the most earnest students of prophecy and the most eager for Christ’s appearing, and they draw on real texts: God has not destined us for wrath (5:9), and believers are to be always ready. Faithful Christians differ here, and the difference does not touch the gospel. Verdict: This passage describes the loudest, most public event imaginable: a shout, an archangel’s voice, God’s trumpet. Nothing is secret. The word meet describes going out to welcome a coming king and escort him back, which points to Christ’s coming to earth, not to a removal to heaven. The same events (trumpet, gathering of the elect, coming on the clouds) describe Christ’s one visible return in Matthew 24:30–31. Scripture teaches one return of Christ, at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, the living changed and caught up, and all are judged (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The rapture is real, but it is part of that one glorious coming, not a separate secret event. This commentary’s wider view is amillennial: the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign between his first and second comings, not a later earthly kingdom, so his one return brings the end. That return is near, yet Paul tells this same church that it will be preceded by named events, the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

Always with the Lord. Here Paul’s own emphasis falls. Not and so we will be in the air, which is merely where the meeting happens. The comfort is not the mechanism but the permanence. What the Thessalonians were frightened of losing, the presence of Christ and each other, turns out to be the one thing that cannot now be interrupted. The heart of the hope is not mainly a place, but a person.

Where will we live forever: in the air, in heaven? With the Lord, wherever he is, and Scripture shows where that will be: a new heaven and a new earth, where the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:1–3; 2 Peter 3:13). The meeting in the air is the welcome on the road, not the final home. Those who die now go to be with Christ in heaven, but the end of the story is a renewed creation, with resurrected people living in resurrected bodies in the presence of God. The air is the meeting place; the new earth is the home.

What about those who are alive when he comes: will they die? No. Paul tells the Corinthians that we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:51–52). Believers alive at his coming will be transformed without passing through death and caught up with the raised dead. Either way, the end is the same: always with the Lord.

Does this mean I should be afraid of being left behind? No. Popular stories about Christians vanishing while others are left to cope have taught many believers to fear, and that is not what this passage gives. There will be no secret disappearance. When Christ comes, every believer, living and dead, will be gathered to him, all at once and in plain sight. If you belong to Christ, you cannot be left behind. The fear this passage should remove is the fear of being forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: “Meet” was the word used of citizens going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him into the city.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another with these words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Encourage one another. The word means to comfort and to exhort. Paul does not say: therefore construct a chart, or work out the sequence, or divide from those who read it differently. This was given to a frightened, bereaved congregation to be used on each other, and our handling of the passage should be measured by that.

One another. Not Paul, who is far away, and not the leaders only: ordinary believers, comforting each other with doctrine. That assumes a congregation where people know each other’s griefs well enough to speak into them, and know the teaching well enough to have something to say.

With these words. Paul expects the actual words to be repeated: at the graveside, in the house afterwards, to the widow in the weeks when everyone else has gone back to normal. The passage ends on being always with the Lord, a sentence built to be said aloud to someone who is crying. It is one of the passages most read at Christian funerals, so Paul’s instruction has been obeyed for nearly two thousand years.

The comfort has a name. The words Paul gives them are not general thoughts about an afterlife. Almost every sentence names Jesus: Jesus died and rose; God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep; the Lord himself will descend; the dead in Christ will rise; we will always be with the Lord. Take his name out and nothing comforting is left. Simeon spent his life waiting for the consolation of Israel and found it as a baby in his arms (Luke 2:25–32). The bereaved of Thessalonica were given the same consolation in words, and it is Christ himself.

What do I actually say to a grieving friend? Usually less than you think, and later than you think. In the first days, presence matters more than words: come, sit, bring food, cry with them (Romans 12:15). Do not explain the loss or hurry them toward feeling better. When the time is right, and especially if the one who died was a believer, say the truth simply: they are with the Lord, and you will see them again; Jesus died and rose, and he will bring them with him. Read these verses together. And keep coming back weeks and months later, when others have stopped.

For worship. The God of all comfort has not left his people to face death with nothing to say. He has given words that can be spoken over every Christian grave, and they have never once failed, because the one they speak of has never once failed. And a day is coming when even these words will not be needed. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4), and the comfort we now speak to one another we will see face to face.
